articles.title: Democrats think a blue wave is building. Here are 3 forces that could stop it
articles.summary: Chuck Schumer says Democrats have "the wind in our sails" ahead of the midterms, but polling errors and GOP money could upend the Senate map.
articles.body: Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer is sounding increasingly bullish about his party's chances of riding a potential blue wave into November, declaring Democrats have "the wind in our sails" as national and battleground polling points to a favorable political environment in the midterm elections. But beneath that confidence are three variables that could determine whether the Democratic advantage becomes a wave — or breaks before Election Day: a potential polling undercount of Republicans, persistent voter skepticism of the Democratic brand, and the GOP’s financial firepower advantage. Schumer, speaking to reporters last week as the Senate adjourned until after Election Day, predicted that Democrats are "on the edge of taking back the Senate." After nearly two years of President Donald Trump back in the White House and Republican control of the Senate and the House, Schumer emphasized, "Americans are frustrated with higher costs and a government they don’t believe is working for them." AI IS SUPERCHARGING THE CAMPAIGN AD WARS, BUT VIRAL DOESN'T MEAN VICTORIOUS The GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the party in power in Washington lose congressional seats during midterm election years. Add to that a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran, and Trump's negative approval ratings. The latest polls indicate Democrats holding an advantage over Republicans in the battle for Congress and that they are more enthusiastic to vote in the midterms. But Trump predicts that Republicans will perform much better in the midterms than critics and pollsters expect. "I think we’re going to have a big surprise, because they don’t know what’s happening," the president told supporters at a rally Saturday night in Ohio, as he referred to Democrats. Here's a closer look at the three variables. Polling problems? Republicans control the Senate 53-47, which means Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority. But with one month to go until Election Day, Democrats are treading deeper and deeper into red territory as Republicans stay mostly on defense. The latest Fox News polls indicate margin of error races in Michigan, a must-hold for the Democrats, and in Texas, Maine and Iowa, three seats the party is working to flip to win the majority. An average of the latest surveys also points to very close contests in Alaska, Ohio and Kansas, where the Democrats are playing offense, and Minnesota, a leading flip opportunity for the GOP. WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM POWER RANKINGS But what if the polls are off? "Polls considerably underestimated Donald Trump and other Republicans on the ticket with him in 2016, 2020, and, to a slightly lesser extent, in 2024," polling guru, political analyst and statistician Nate Silver noted this past weekend. But Silver added that polls in the previous two Trump-era midterms, 2018 and 2022, were essentially unbiased. Fast-forward to this cycle, and polls in some high-profile Democratic primaries were off the mark. Among the miscues this summer: overestimating Abdul El-Sayed's narrow victory in Michigan's Senate showdown, and underestimating victories by Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota's Senate primary, state Rep. Angie Nixon's win in Florida's Senate contest, and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley's upset victory to capture the Wisconsin gubernatorial nomination. Coverage of the miscues grabbed widespread media attention and sparked fresh criticism of public opinion polling. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB If the surveys are overestimating Democratic turnout and underestimating Republican enthusiasm, even a modest polling miss could reshape several of the close Senate contests. "I don't think any Democrat is over optimistic after … 2024. We all understand that anything can happen in the closing days, and we're preparing for that," longtime New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Ray Buckley told Fox News Digital. Bad brand? Trump's approval ratings remain well underwater, as do favorable ratings for the GOP. But surveys indicate the Democrats' brand is nothing to brag about. The Democrats' favorable rating hovered in negative territory in the most recent Fox News national poll, at 44%-55%. And it was even lower in the latest Wall Street Journal national survey, at 38% favorable and 58% unfavorable. "I think just because Americans are outraged because of how Republicans have failed them and made their life more expensive doesn't automatically mean that they're going to embrace and trust Democrats," former Biden administration Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg told Fox News Digital on Saturday. Buttigieg, a 2020 Democratic presidential candidate who is considering another White House run in 2028, said it's crucial Democrats "make sure that our candidates get out there, make it very clear who they are, what they're about, and what we would do differently." Making life even tougher for the Democrats: the victories by left-wing and socialist-aligned candidates over more moderate contenders in the party's primaries, which gave the GOP more messaging ammunition to portray all Democrats on the ballot this year as radicals. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER That's the case in Michigan, Minnesota and Florida, where El-Sayed, Flanagan and Nixon all defeated establishment-backed rivals. Meanwhile, in Texas, a trail of controversial past comments by Talarico is handing the GOP more firepower. But Democrats in all four of these Senate showdowns are returning fire by anchoring the Republicans on the ballot to Trump. In the latest Fox News poll in Texas, 53% of those questioned said they were extremely or very concerned that Talarico is too liberal. But a near equal amount, 51%, said they were extremely or very concerned that Paxton is too close to Trump. Money matters Republicans are winning the ad wars, thanks to a major money advantage. Boosted by massive cash infusions from the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. and other leading Republican groups and donors, the GOP is outspending the Democrats in all the crucial Senate showdowns. That includes a roughly $70 million advantage in Ohio and nearly $30 million in Maine and Texas, three top targets for the Democrats, according to figures from AdImpact, a top ad-tracking firm. The GOP's outspending the Democrats by approximately $25 million in Michigan, which Republicans are aiming to flip. Republicans are also outspending Democrats in swing state New Hampshire, in the battle to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. "The amount of money being spent is enormous," Buckley told Fox News Digital, as he pointed to all the Republican-aligned ads flooding the small state. "We might not be as competitive as we'd like on television, but we're certainly competitive knocking on the doors. We've got the energy out there. The voters are excited. You saw that with the turnout in the primaries throughout the country," he said.

articles.body:
Two decades after joining the Supreme Court, Justice Samuel Alito joins the ranks of justices as authors.

Alito’s first book, “So Ordered,” set for release Tuesday, is an adapted collection of speeches he’s given over the years commenting on abortion, originalism, threats to the judiciary and more.

It doesn’t break much new ground for those who’ve closely followed the conservative justice’s every word with bated breath. Still, Tuesday’s launch thrusts Alito further into the public limelight at a time when the Supreme Court is beginning another term packed with politically charged cases, all while pollsters indicate a majority of the public hasn’t heard enough to form an opinion of the justice.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“Today, freedom of speech on important subjects is in greater danger than at any prior time in my lifetime,” Alito wrote in his adapted 2017 speech to a conservative think tank.

Adapting a 2024 speech he gave at a Catholic university, Alito wrote, “Many students don’t want to hear arguments they find objectionable. And many others are afraid of speaking freely.”

“Let judges be judges. For if they are not, our legal system, as we know it, will fade away,” he said in an adaptation of a 2010 speech.

Unlike some of his colleagues who signed book deals soon after joining the Supreme Court, the project marks Alito’s first published book since being nominated by then-President George W. Bush in 2005. The justice, long described by former colleagues and friends as introverted, has yet to announce any extensive book tour.

Alito declined The Hill’s request to be interviewed for this story.

“So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country” spans speeches Alito has given dating back to 2007 through last year. It includes talks at law schools, bar association events and judicial conferences.

“They were not composed with the idea that they would eventually be woven together into a book,” Alito writes.

Relatively few justices — Ketanji Brown Jackson, Ruth Bader Ginsburg and John Paul Stevens — have published transcripts of their prepared speeches online afterward. And Alito has not, leaving a scattering of media reports and an occasional recording. Among Alito’s selections is a 2021 speech he gave at Notre Dame Law School responding to criticisms of the Supreme Court’s emergency docket, which erupted in activity during the first Trump administration and the COVID-19 pandemic. Though his comments were livestreamed, the school didn’t post a recording . Unofficial accounts had since “circulate[d] like samizdat” among scholars, one professor wrote in a law review article published earlier this year.

The book also notably includes Alito’s virtual address delivered a year prior to the annual convention of the Federalist Society, the conservative legal group. It drew condemnation from his critics after Alito said the pandemic had caused “previously unimaginable” restrictions on civil liberties. In the book, it’s part of a section titled “Threats to the Constitution.”

“The Covid crisis has served as a sort of constitutional stress test,” Alito wrote in his adaptation of that 2020 speech. “And in doing so, it has highlighted disturbing trends that were already present before the virus struck, trends that we must resist and reverse when the crisis is over.”

Alito, a key member of the Supreme Court’s 6-3 conservative majority, doesn’t shy away from the culture wars or some of the court’s most controversial decisions in his speeches and the book. He’s arguably most known for authoring the 2022 decision overturning Roe v. Wade, which had established a constitutional right to abortion.

Speaking with “Fox News Sunday,” Alito said he had anticipated the decision would anger “many people.”

“I wasn’t surprised that there was such a reaction. I didn’t anticipate the particulars,” Alito said, noting his draft majority opinion was leaked, and his colleague, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, faced an assassination attempt at his home.

The Supreme Court has never publicly identified the leaker, saying it can’t find a person responsible under a “preponderance of the evidence” standard.

Alito has long publicly suggested he has someone in mind . His book launch renewed the question, and the justice isn’t suggesting his views have changed.

“I do have an opinion. But the evidence available at this time is not strong enough for the court or for me to say this is the person who was responsible,” Alito told “Fox News Sunday.”

Despite the abortion decision’s continued prominence in American life, Alito remains the third least-known justice, polling data shows.

According to a July Marquette Law School poll, 34 percent of adults said they hadn’t heard of him, a figure only surpassed by Justices Neil Gorsuch and Elena Kagan. Another 27 percent said they hadn’t heard enough about Alito to form an opinion. The poll had a margin of error of 3.2 percentage points.

As he entered the courtroom for the start of his 22nd term Monday, Alito quickly took his seat without looking out at the gallery.

He had recused from the first case of the term, a blockbuster state-court lawsuit against fossil fuel producers, and was joining his eight colleagues already on the bench. Alito — yellow legal pad in hand — was seen laughing and nodding along as Chief Justice John Roberts whispered something to him during the break before the second case began.

Alito, now 76, has faced increasing retirement speculation in recent years. Some of the pressure has come from Republicans, who had hoped they’d be able to confirm a successor before the midterm elections, when Democrats hope to flip the Senate.

Alito confirmed to CBS News that he had “thought about” retirement this past term and he would continue to do so annually. But as of now, he’s staying put.

“It’s something, I think, that somebody at my age has to think about every term,” he said. “But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place.”

articles.body:
We’re now over the hump and into the downhill slide to the end of the 2026 midterm elections. I say “end” because early voting has already begun in six states, and by the end of next week, the number will be up to 19 and counting.

A mighty river of ballots, eventually more than 100 million in all, is forming from these modest tributaries. About half will have been cast before Nov. 3, when the final deluge comes in. That’s all well and good — the pageant of democracy and all that jazz — but what people really want to know is which ballots.

Midterms are mostly a matter of subtraction. There were 155,552,842 valid ballots cast in the 2024 presidential election — about 64 percent of the voting-eligible population . In recent history, midterm turnout has tended to be about a third less than in presidential cycles, which would put this year on track for a respectable 103 million or so.

The massively high turnout of the 2020 presidential election — at more than two-thirds of eligible voters , it was the highest in the modern, post-Voting Rights Act era — can be in large part attributed to the pandemic. Not only did temporary mail-in and early voting rules make it easier for people to cast ballots, Americans were very upset in fall 2020, and when times are bad, turnout is good. Plus, people had a lot of free time on their hands.

But we can’t chalk all of the 2020 surge up to COVID-19 and the social unrest of that ugly year. That’s because the prepandemic 2018 midterm elections were an absolute barn-burner for turnout. Something like half of eligible voters participated in the Trump I midterms, about as high of a percentage that showed up in some presidential election years in the palmy days of the late 1980s and the 1990s. Good times make for bad turnout.

Turnout dropped in the 2022 midterms compared to 2018, ticking down to about 45 percent — but still well ahead of the laughably low 34.4 percent in 2014. Basically, 2022 showed the American electorate getting back to its normal midterm turnout, which has typically bounced around in the low 40s. Indeed, the story of the 2010s is a very typical midterm boom-and-bust cycle.

Then-President Obama won big in 2008, sweeping many red-state Democrats along with him. Many in the Obama coalition, including a big chunk of new voters, sat out the 2010 midterms and Republicans took back all they had lost and then some. Obama had a solid, but less sweeping win in his 2012 reelection. It was still enough to help pare back some of the GOP’s midterm gains. Then in 2014, the bottom dropped out for Democrats. Though 2010 is remembered for the Tea Party wave and the massive House gains for Republicans — the most for any party since World War II — it was actually 2014 when Republicans hit their highest heights.

The 30-seat GOP House majority and a jaw-dropping nine Senate seat flips — the most since 1946 — were the result of many factors, but none so much as the fact that so many Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents stayed home. That rock-bottom 2014 turnout number was a great big shrug emoji from the Obama coalition. It was a foreshadowing of the 2016 presidential election in which turnout lagged and a Republican pulled off the most astonishing upset in presidential politics since at least then-President Truman’s 1948 comeback.

Democrats, whether they were disillusioned by eight years in power, dissatisfied with their own nominee or complacent because the Republicans had nominated a foul-mouthed reality show host, dropped the ball.

After his first election, President Trump has been the greatest vehicle for voter mobilization in our lifetimes. That first win would have been a fluke, if not for the fact that once he had power, Trump and Trumpism profoundly affected voter intensity. Unfortunately for Republicans, that applies to both parties. The simplest way to understand the turnout surge since 2018 is that Trump brings voters out of the woodwork: lower-propensity, mostly white working-class voters who love the guy and the college-educated, high-propensity suburbanites who hate him like God hates sin.

So how will that work in the sixth and final election of the Trump era?

Republicans know that if there’s a typical dropoff — say 42 million fewer votes than two years ago — the absent voters will disproportionately be members of their party and sympathetic independents. This is why the president is raiding the federal treasury to run campaign ads for himself, sending checks to voters and promising much bigger payouts if Republicans stay in power. He’s barnstorming red states and, as promised, running like he’s on the ballot himself.

The scenario Republicans most fear is one in which there’s a second-midterm dropoff for Trump’s coalition like the ones that afflicted Obama and former President George W. Bush before him. Bush’s 2006 catastrophe is the one that’s haunting many in the GOP right now: high gas prices, an unpopular war and a sense of disorder in Washington. But what’s different now is that Democrats are mobilized in a way that exceeds that year or even the blue wave of 2018.

In the 21st century, primary election turnout has been probably the most reliable predictor of partisan turnout trends in general elections — not for each individual race but taken as a whole. In 2018, Democratic primary turnout was 8 points higher than it was for Republicans. This year, the margin swelled to 11 points .

We know for certain that Democrats are going to vote at very high rates. Every measurement we have suggests that the blue wave has already formed. What we don’t know is what it’s going to be crashing into. That’s why Republicans are going to spend the next four weeks wheedling, cajoling and even outright paying their missing voters to crank it up one more time for Trump.

articles.title: Trump’s feud with Cotton snaps heads in the Senate
articles.summary: President Trump’s doxing of Sen. Tom Cotton over a stalled bill to establish year-round daylight saving time is throwing an unexpected twist in the Arkansas Republican’s reelection race and sets up a fierce fight in the Senate this fall over the biannual changing of clocks. Trump’s decision to publish Cotton’s cellphone number on his Truth…
articles.body:
President Trump’s doxing of Sen. Tom Cotton over a stalled bill to establish year-round daylight saving time is throwing an unexpected twist in the Arkansas Republican’s reelection race and sets up a fierce fight in the Senate this fall over the biannual changing of clocks.

Trump’s decision to publish Cotton’s cellphone number on his Truth Social account, which has more than 13 million followers, left Senate Republicans and their advisers in shock.

Trump urged his followers to press Cotton, the third-ranking member of the Senate GOP leadership and the chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, to contact the senator directly to press him to drop his opposition to the Sunshine Protection Act.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

One Senate Republican strategist called Trump’s doxing of Cotton, one of the most influential national security hawks in the Republican conference, an “enormous disruption.” The strategist questioned whether the president is throwing a brushback pitch at a rising conservative star who may be the next Senate GOP leader trying to get him in line.

“The chairman of the Select Committee on Intelligence gets a lot of important calls. I imagine he’s had to turn that phone off and contact known associates with a new phone number. It is mind-bogglingly stupid of this administration in the midst of a disastrous campaign to focus on this,” said the GOP strategist, who requested anonymity to comment on Trump’s shot at Cotton.

“It’s not like the Senate can suddenly come back into session and pass this bill,” the GOP strategist said. “Tom Cotton has a pretty good argument for why he doesn’t like the bill.

“Whichever stupid staffer that put this in front of [the president] did not think about the fact that for the next two years you’re going to need ever single Senate Republican to band together against impeachment, against subpoenas,” the source said, noting that Republicans are expected to lose Senate seats — and possibly their majority — next month.

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) defended Cotton’s opposition to making daylight saving time permanent as driven by “real safety concerns.”

Wicker said Cotton is speaking for a number of Republican senators when he stands up against making daylight saving time year-round.

“I think there’s more opposition to it than the president realizes. There’s some real safety concerns, particularly in the more northern and rural states where children get on the school bus at very early hours,” Wicker said.

And Wicker said he “wouldn’t have advised” Trump to make Cotton’s cellphone number public, which will probably force the third-ranking member of the Senate GOP leadership to find a new number.

“I wouldn’t have advised to do that,” he said.

The battle in the Senate over making daylight saving time year-round will reach a critical point during the Senate’s lame-duck session in November and December.

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), another close Trump ally, is working hard behind the scenes to get a vote on the Sunshine Protection Act, which passed the House 308-117 in July.

“I’ve got my Sunshine Protection Act. I’m working on a vote on that. We’re going to have a vote on that. It [lets] states make their own decisions,” he told The Hill.

Scott emphasized the bill doesn’t require states to permanently adopt daylight saving time but gives them the option of doing so.

The idea is very popular in his home state of Florida, where, according to one GOP strategist, it has overwhelming support.

But senators who represent northern states and those on the western edges of the Central and Mountain time zones are not fans of the idea, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.).

“I’m from a northern clime,” Thune said. “I voted against it in committee,” referring to his opposition as a member of the Senate Commerce Committee.

Thune said it “remains to be seen” whether the Sunshine Protection Act could get the 60 votes it needs to pass the Senate.

One former GOP aide hypothesized that Trump in a subtle way may be trying to exert some influence on a future Senate leadership race.

“This might be a way for him to s‑‑‑ on Cotton’s leadership race,” the source said, speculating that Cotton could make a bid for leader if Thune decides to retire after this year’s election.

Both Cotton and Scott are viewed as potential candidates to become the next Senate Republican leader whenever Thune, who is 65, decides to step down from the job.

When asked about the online clash between Trump and Cotton, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) quipped that the president “can go from zero to a‑‑hole in about three seconds.”

“Tom Cotton feels strongly about it. Tom is a rock star senator. If you get between him and what’s best for Arkansas, he’ll devour you like a light snack,” Kennedy told Kristen Welker on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

“President Trump’s also my friend. He feels strongly about it,” he continued. “The president, as we know, can be sometimes — he exists loudly. He can be tempestuous,” he added.

A senior Senate Republican aide who requested anonymity to discuss the controversy said that “nothing” that Trump does really surprises senators but acknowledged that any Senate chief of staff would be highly annoyed and agitated if someone blasted out their boss’s cellphone number to millions of people.

Trump pulled a similar move on then-Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) in 2015 when he read the South Carolina Republican’s cellphone number out to a crowd at a speech in South Carolina.

Trump shared Graham’s private number with the world hours after Graham called him a “jacka‑‑.”

Graham then published a video of himself destroying his old flip phone in a variety of creative ways, chopping it with a meat cleaver, dropping it into a blender and walloping it with a golf driver.

Cotton also appeared to take Trump’s publication of his private information in stride — but he held firm to his opposition to the legislation that would encourage states to adopt daylight saving time all year long.

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” he posted on social platform X over the weekend.

“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” he said.

The high-profile clash throws a twist into Cotton’s otherwise unnoticed reelection campaign.

The two-term Republican incumbent is running comfortably ahead of his little-known Democratic opponent, Hallie Shoffner, a sixth-generation farmer, in an August poll of 803 likely voters by J.L. Partners.

Other polls, however, show the race could be more competitive than expected.

A Hendrix College poll of 1,217 likely voters conducted Aug. 11-12 showed Shoffner leading Cotton 47 percent to 44 percent.

But hardly any Senate Democrats are talking about Arkansas as a real opportunity to pick up a Republican seat in November, even if there is a big blue wave that propels them to the majority.

articles.title: Mamdani’s plan to tackle antisemitism faces backlash from Jewish New Yorkers
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) rolled out a first-of-its-kind municipal strategy to combat antisemitism last week, and it has drawn some criticism from Jewish leaders who say its omission of Israel and anti-Zionism overlooks a key factor behind the recent rise in hate crimes against Jewish New Yorkers. A joint statement from the…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) rolled out a first-of-its-kind municipal strategy to combat antisemitism last week, and it has drawn some criticism from Jewish leaders who say its omission of Israel and anti-Zionism overlooks a key factor behind the recent rise in hate crimes against Jewish New Yorkers.

A joint statement from the United Jewish Appeal (UJA)-Federation of New York, the Jewish Community Relations Council of New York, the American Jewish Committee, and the New York Board of Rabbis welcomed elements of the plan but said the city must also confront anti-Israel rhetoric — including Mamdani’s own — to effectively combat antisemitism.

“While the Mayor’s plan has a number of positive elements, including some increased security funding for Jewish institutions and expanding proven programs, it fails to address a central issue that the Mayor himself has perpetuated: rhetoric that demonizes and delegitimizes Israel inevitably leads to the targeting of Jewish New Yorkers,” the groups wrote in a statement .

The strategy highlights the $1 million allocated in Mamdani’s budget to bolster security at synagogues and other houses of worship, and $6.4 million for Partners Against the Hate grants to community organizations that focus on hate prevention, data collection and survivor support.

The initiative also expands Holocaust and Jewish history education, and strengthens coordination among city agencies on community outreach and access to security funding.

“Antisemitism has no place in New York City. Jewish New Yorkers have helped build this city, shaped its culture and strengthened our communities for generations, and they deserve to be safe, celebrated and protected by a city government that stands with them,” Mamdani said in a statement unveiling the strategy.

Mamdani has faced criticism over his own rhetoric about Israel. In a July 21 video , he acknowledged that he lacked the authority to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if he visited the city, despite repeatedly pledging to do so. After a Jewish man was stabbed on the Upper West Side two days later in what police investigated as an antisemitic hate crime, Jewish leaders urged the mayor to temper his rhetoric about Israel. Mamdani condemned the attack at the time.

Pamela Nadell, author of “Antisemitism, An American Tradition,” told The Hill she thinks it’s “commendable” that the city launched the first municipal-level strategy, and applauded the whole-of-government approach, its objectives and its focus on education. But she criticized the strategy for naming examples of attacks on Jews with roots on the right — like the march in Charlottesville, Va., and the Tree of Life synagogue shooting in Pittsburgh — while “absolutely ignor[ing] it when it comes from the left.”

“This just happens both on the right and the left. They’re more than willing to see Jew-hatred when it’s coming from the other side of the political aisle. They refuse to acknowledge it when it’s in their own camp,” said Nadell, a professor of women’s and gender history and director of the Jewish Studies program at American University.

There are some exceptions to that rule, Nadell said, but the “reality is that antisemitism is coming from both sides of the political aisle at this moment, which is what makes it so fraught for the Jewish community.”

Hate crimes against Jews in New York City rose 8 percent in the first half of this year compared with the same period last year, according to data from the New York Police Department.

Jews were targeted in 229 of the 425 reported hate crimes, more than all other groups combined. Another 46 crimes were based on sexual orientation, 36 fell under the generic “religion” category, 29 targeted Black people and 27 targeted Muslims. No other category had more than 18 reported incidents.

A group of 25 New York City-based Jewish groups signed on to a letter Friday criticizing the report, which they said, “reaches back eight years to highlight right-wing terrorist attacks in other cities, while failing to discuss, or even mention, a single anti-Jewish incident that occurred in New York in the past three years,” according to reports from the New York Post and The Jerusalem Post .

“Our community generally isn’t encountering Charlottesville-style white supremacists in our neighborhoods,” the letter read, according to the reports. Instead, the groups wrote, Jewish New Yorkers face “anti-Zionist animus that too often veers into anti-Jewish harassment, exclusion, and even violence.”

Ari Berman, president of Yeshiva University in New York, said the plan includes “ some positive steps ,” but called the mayor “an arsonist posing as a firefighter” and urged him to roll back his anti-Israel comments and “acknowledge the damage his rhetoric has done.”

Ammiel Hirsch, president of the New York Board of Rabbis, has talked to Mamdani about the effect he sees the mayor’s anti-Israel rhetoric having on the city’s Jewish community but said he sees “a reluctance on his part to forgo the ability to deny Israel’s right to exist, what he calls anti-Zionism.”

Hirsch, senior rabbi at the Stephen Wise Free Synagogue, a prominent Reform congregation on the Upper West Side, said while anti-Zionism is not the same as antisemitism, there is “about 120 years of history that establishes, without a shadow of a doubt, that anti-Zionist hostility creates antisemitic, anti-Jewish hostility. You can’t separate the two.”

“The idea that you could write a serious report and seriously attempt to lower the surge in antisemitism in New York City by completely ignoring the primary driver of antisemitism in New York City now — which is obsessive loathing of Israel — is just unserious,” he said, stressing that Israeli policies themselves are “of course legitimately subject to critique and opposition.”

Asked about criticism that the report fails to address Israel or anti-Zionism, Phylisa Wisdom, the executive director of the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism, said the administration’s strategy “reflects the Mamdani administration’s commitment to rooting out antisemitism in all its forms.”

“Every Jewish New Yorker, no matter their views, deserves to live safely and proudly as themselves in our city,” she said in a statement to The Hill, adding, “Rather than defining Jewish identity or Jewish communities’ relationship to these topics for them, or weighing in on intramural debates, we see our administration’s responsibility as delivering safety and a sense of inclusion, regardless of their views on them.”

The strategy has separately drawn criticism for intentionally declining to adopt a definition of antisemitism.

A statement from Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center, a Jewish human rights group, said “a strategy to combat antisemitism has to be able to state plainly what is being combatted,” noting a standard can be especially important in determining when rhetoric against Israel crosses into rhetoric against Jewish people.

“Without that clarity, an important question remains: What standard will New York City use to determine when rhetoric or conduct crosses into antisemitism, particularly when ‘Zionist’ becomes a proxy for Jew or when Jewish New Yorkers are targeted because of their connection to Israel?” Berk wrote.

Kenneth Stern, director of the Bard Center for the Study of Hate, called the strategy a good first step and praised many of its objectives, but he said he disagreed with criticism over its lack of a definition. He was the lead drafter in 2004 of the European Monitoring Centre on Racism and Xenophobia (EUMC) definition of antisemitism, which was later adopted by the State Department and by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) in 2016.

Stern said embracing a single definition could lead to getting bogged down in the details of what counts as antisemitism rather than looking more broadly at its effect on society. He also noted that much of the Jewish community disagrees on a single definition, arguing it would be unwise for elected officials to set one.

“I think it’s terribly inappropriate for the government to decide this. I don’t like Jewish groups basically asking the government to decide,” Stern told The Hill.

“That’s an internal question of how we deal with the future of the Jewish community, how we understand anti-Zionism inside the community,” he said, adding, “That’s, again, something that’s never worked out well for minorities, Jews included, historically.”

articles.title: Dem fundraising giant makes damning admission as GOP probes foreign donation allegations
articles.summary: ActBlue launched a new passport verification program days after House GOP investigators accused the platform of potentially accepting foreign donations.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Democrats' largest campaign fundraising platform says it has strengthened its donor verification standards days after House GOP investigators accused it of potentially taking in foreign donations for U.S. campaigns, according to a new letter obtained by Fox News Digital. Attorneys for ActBlue sent a letter to the House of Representatives on Monday announcing it is launching a new "passport verification program" as part of its "ongoing investment in the security of contributions processed from donors located abroad." House Republicans have for years accused ActBlue of having insufficient verification standards for weeding out illegitimate campaign donations. The platform has long been used by a myriad of Democrats to raise money for their political campaigns, including Democratic leaders in the House and Senate. ActBlue said it paused donations from Americans abroad in 2025, however. REPUBLICANS ZERO IN ON KEY PLAYER ACCUSED OF HELPING DEMOCRAT FUNDRAISING GIANT HIDE FOREIGN CASH ActBlue has consistently denied wrongdoing in responses to Fox News Digital and communications to House investigators. Ten top figures within the company, including executives and founders, have pleaded the Fifth Amendment to avoid answering questions in both public and private sitdowns with GOP-led committees. ANOTHER ACTBLUE LEADER PLEADS FIFTH AS HOUSE INVESTIGATES ALLEGED FOREIGN DONATIONS But a new report released earlier this month, first reported by Fox News Digital, appears to show employees green-lighting donations despite some questions about where they came from. Chief among the GOP's concerns is ActBlue's passport number verification. According to the report, the field only required the correct number of characters for a U.S. passport number rather than a valid code for a donation to be accepted. GOP LAWMAKER WARNS ACTBLUE 'GOT CAUGHT' AS FOREIGN CASH PROBE TRIGGERS FIFTH AMENDMENT PLEAS But the Monday letter said ActBlue's new program "adds passport-based identity verification as a further enhancement to ActBlue’s multi-layered approach to fraud and foreign-contribution prevention." "In doing so, it also enables U.S. citizens located abroad—who have been unable to contribute on the ActBlue platform since 2025—to resume participating in the political process by supporting the candidates and causes of their choice," the letter said. "The new program uses the best available technology to allow eligible donors located abroad to verify their identity using a valid U.S. passport. It reflects substantial engineering investments by ActBlue to ensure that, as it resumes processing contributions from foreign addresses, its compliance systems can withstand scrutiny." Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., said it amounted to a confession. "This decision to implement a NEW passport verification program only confirms what we've been saying: ActBlue failed to verify the citizenship of individuals who made donations from abroad. That's unacceptable," Steil told Fox News Digital. "This new policy should have been in place on day one. Right now, far too many questions remain unanswered, including what percentage of the billions of dollars that have flowed through ActBlue came from illegal foreign sources. Chairman Jordan, Chairman Comer, and I will continue to seek answers for the American people." ACTBLUE SCRUTINY FUELS NEW GOP BILLS TO TIGHTEN ELECTION DONATION RULES The probe is being co-led by his panel as well as House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky. A spokesperson for Jordan told Fox News Digital, "This action confirms that the platform's fraud prevention measures were not as robust as [ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones] told Congress. We will continue to demand answers." The GOP's earlier report cited a letter by Wallace-Jones to Steil, which maintained that donations on the platform made by people with addresses outside the U.S. required a passport number for verification. But the Republicans' report alleged that the verification "only ensures that the entered passport number contains a certain number of characters, not that it is a valid U.S. passport number," rendering it an essentially meaningless step. ActBlue told Fox News Digital in response to the report at the time, "There’s nothing to see here. After we released findings of a third-party forensic analysis that completely undermined a central claim that they have made against ActBlue, Republicans are refusing to move on." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Instead, they are orchestrating another political stunt before rushing out of town weeks early to go campaign. This coordinated campaign against ActBlue isn’t about the facts, or legislating, it’s about Republicans’ efforts to silence organizations they believe threaten their agenda," the platform said. A spokesperson for ActBlue pointed Fox News Digital to a blog post announcing the update when reached for comment. "In 2025, amid unprecedented attacks from President Trump and his allies, our organization took the proactive step of temporarily suspending all contributions from outside the United States," the statement said. "ActBlue has now further enhanced its verification process to allow eligible Americans with a U.S. Passport who are located abroad to participate through the platform while maintaining the robust security and compliance standards that donors, campaign, and the public expect." It also said ActBlue "accurately described" its vetting process to Congress.

articles.title: Let the debates begin: 5 to watch this week
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Supreme Court back in session ▪ Trump touts diesel executive order ▪ Politico blocked from Air Force One ▪ Russia outbreak fuels concern General election debate season kicks into high gear this week with candidates meeting on stages throughout the country in races up and down the ticket. Today marks exactly…
articles.body:
General election debate season kicks into high gear this week with candidates meeting on stages throughout the country in races up and down the ticket.

Today marks exactly four weeks until Election Day and the first in a string of major faceoffs running through Friday. Several of them are for statewide Senate and governor races, while others are taking place in critical battleground House districts that could decide which party wins a majority.

Here are five of the most consequential debates to watch this week:

One of the most pivotal Senate races for Democrats if they are to win back control of the upper chamber is knocking off Sen. Susan Collins (R) in Maine.

Collins will face off against former state Senate President Troy Jackson , the Democratic nominee, for the first time tonight at 7 p.m. Jackson has had a long journey already, having run an unsuccessful gubernatorial bid earlier this year before quickly clinching his party’s nod for Senate after Graham Platner dropped out amid various controversies.

Now, Jackson is hoping to put the longtime senator on the defensive, as he has sought to tie her to President Trump ‘s agenda. Collins has emphasized her independent streak and track record of directing federal money to the state.

The two candidates will meet again on Thursday at 8 p.m.

Despite the race taking place in a state that has mostly voted blue in federal races, polls suggest a tight race .

The Hawkeye State has moved away from Democrats in recent years, but the party is hoping to return to its former success if a blue wave materializes.

State Auditor Rob Sand , the only Democrat elected to statewide office four years ago, is perhaps the biggest source of optimism for his party in Iowa. Sand has been comfortably leading Republican Zach Lahn in polls for the governor’s race for months.

They’re trying to succeed outgoing Gov. Kim Reynolds (R), who won two terms but is one of the least popular governors in the country.

Still, Democrats can’t afford to get complacent in a state that has increasingly moved away from them in recent years. Lahn, a businessman, has promoted himself as an outsider to politics, while Sand has accused him of being a carpetbagger over his ties to Kansas.

Sand and Lahn will take to the debate stage at 8 p.m. EDT in Davenport.

Democrats are running it back in an open district in Arizona with the same candidate as two years ago against a longtime former NFL kicker.

Rep. David Schweikert (R) passed on a reelection bid this year for an unsuccessful run for governor, leaving Arizona’s 1st District open. Democrats renominated former state Rep. Amish Shah , who lost to Schweikert by a few points in 2024, while Republicans turned to Jay Feely , who played for more than a half-dozen NFL teams over a 14-year career.

Shah and Feely will face each other at 8 p.m. EDT Wednesday. While this is the first time they will appear together as candidates, it won’t be the first time their paths crossed.

They previously worked for the New York Jets simultaneously during the 2008 and 2009 seasons, when Feely was the team’s kicker and Shah was the team doctor.

On the other side of the coin, Republicans are looking to pick up a seat against the incumbent in Washington’s 3rd District.

Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) has been at odds with her party on a few occasions, most recently when she and Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) crossed party lines to help the GOP advance a few of their legislative priorities.

Still, Democrats would much rather have her in the caucus than handing the seat to Republicans. She’s facing state Senate Minority Leader John Braun (R).

Republicans are hoping they could finally have an opportunity in this district after the party’s previous nominee, Joe Kent , lost two races in a row in 2022 and 2024.

One key aspect to watch is how Gluesenkamp Perez describes her role within her party, given her sometimes independent streak. She and Braun will debate at 10 p.m. EDT on Wednesday, hosted by the Nexstar affiliate KOIN. Nexstar also owns The Hill.

Michigan represents one of the few opportunities for the GOP to go on offense in the Senate, and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) will try to seize the momentum from Democrat Abdul El-Sayed at 7 p.m. Thursday.

The debate will be hosted by Nexstar affiliate WOOD, which is based in Grand Rapids.

Polling has shown a close race between the candidates, though El-Sayed has narrowly led in the Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) polling average since mid-August.

Rogers has sought to depict El-Sayed as far left and emphasized the nominee’s connections to the controversial political streamer Hasan Piker . El-Sayed has accused Rogers of being a yes-man for the president and corporate interests.

Rogers skipped one planned debate last month, leaving the stage to El-Sayed alone, but the two are expected to be present face-to-face for the first time this week.

▪ The Hill : Pete Hegseth ’s get-out-the-vote effort draws mixed response.

▪ The Hill Insider : Trump’s deportation agenda haunts him in two House races.

Speaking of the DDHQ polling average , be sure to check out The Hill’s new webpage dedicated to all the news, polling and forecast models ahead of the midterm races with Election Day fast approaching. And sign up for Insider for access to all data and election tools needed for a full picture of where the races stand.

The president said he will pay for his controversial “Patriotic Ads” with money raised for his super PAC, MAGA Inc., following backlash over the government-funded commercials touting his administration and denouncing socialism and communism. Critics argued the ads were an improper use of taxpayer dollars, and some Democrats had called for an investigation into them.

Trump has approved the death penalty to be carried out by firing squad against former Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan for the 2009 Fort Hood shooting in Texas that claimed 13 lives and injured 30 others. The shooting was the deadliest mass shooting on a U.S. military base in history. The military hasn’t carried out a death sentence since 1961.

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is slated to join Fox News as a contributor on Nov. 1. Leavitt left her role as the president’s top spokesperson at the start of September, saying she wanted to spend more time with family shortly after giving birth to her second child.

Climate activists gather outside the Supreme Court as the Supreme Court hears arguments in Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, Oct. 5, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta)

BACK IN SESSION : The Supreme Court opened its first day of the new term with oral arguments in a major climate case that could determine the future of state and local efforts to recover damages from fossil fuel companies over their role in global warming.

The Hill’s Rachel Frazin reports that several justices appeared unconvinced of the companies’ request for the high court to toss out a ruling from the Colorado Supreme Court allowing a lawsuit to proceed. It aims to hold Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil accountable for climate-related damages.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson questioned Suncor Energy lawyer Kannon Shanmugam over whether it’s premature for the court to even hear the case at this point. Conservative Justices John Roberts and Neil Gorsuch similarly asked the fossil fuel firm tough questions.

“A number of the discussions that you’ve had with my colleagues make me think that we’re really early in this case – that this is sort of premature from the standpoint of this court exercising its jurisdiction,” Jackson said.

Shanmugam said the planet-warming emissions are not necessarily directed at Colorado and argued Colorado state law should not apply to actions of companies operating outside the state. But Roberts pushed the lawyer on that argument, invoking a scenario in which someone in one state tries to throw a rock over a state border but unintentionally hits someone in a third state.

“If you’re in [State] B and you’re aiming at [State] C, but you hit somebody in [State] A, that doesn’t make a difference, does it?” Roberts asked.

But the chief justice also asked how the lawsuit, if allowed to proceed, would feasibly work, saying, “Presumably, if you prevail, the next day, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit.”

“There’s always going to be greenhouse gas emissions affecting every state,” Roberts added.

Boulder needs only four votes in its favor to win the case, since conservative Justice Samuel Alito recused himself. The fossil fuel firms would need five justices to side with them, since a split decision means the lower court’s ruling would stand.

SEEING RED : Trump signed an executive order Monday to increase the availability of red-dyed diesel to address the high cost of the fuel.

This diesel isn’t different from regular diesel but is dyed red to signal that it is tax-exempt. It’s typically used in machines such as farm and construction equipment.

Trump said this order should save farmers “millions.” He announced the decision during a rally in Nebraska to support Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.).

Tom Kloza , the chief oil analyst for Gulf Oil, told Frazin that he doesn’t expect the move to make a significant difference in the overall price of diesel, calling it a “Band-Aid.”

The average price of a gallon of diesel has dropped a bit in recent days, though it currently sits at more than $6.30 , well above its level before the start of the Iran war earlier this year.

ACCESS DENIED : The White House refused to allow journalists from Politico to board Air Force One on Monday, blocking the news outlet from fulfilling its pool duties to cover the president on his trip to Nebraska.

Washington Post reporter Katherine Doyle was allowed on the plane as the “secondary” travel print pooler, but the primary print pooler is the one who typically sends updates to other outlets.

“Since it [the White House] was unable to find a replacement, there is no primary print pooler on this trip,” she wrote in an email to colleagues.

Politico is one of three outlets — along with MS NOW and CNN — that Trump blocked from the White House last month, sparking a lawsuit on First Amendment grounds.

A federal judge ruled the administration violated the outlets’ due process rights, and journalists from the outlets were eventually allowed back into the White House. But the administration has since sought to keep CNN from carrying out its TV press pool duties on two occasions.

NEW CRYPTO RULES: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) unveiled new proposals for regulating cryptocurrency markets, giving notice of its plans to move forward with rulemaking on both crypto asset transactions and markets.

The planned rules, which come just weeks after lawmakers failed to pass digital asset legislation through Congress, would outline how existing commodities law applies to transactions involving digital assets and would establish a new type of exchange that can register with the CFTC for the purpose of trading the assets.

CFTC Chair Michael Selig made clear that the intention is to create a “federal option for crypto asset exchanges” but would not require all to register with the agency.

“Only Congress has the authority to mandate that all crypto asset exchanges register with the Commission,” he said at Fordham Law School yesterday, according to his prepared remarks.

SHATTERED LEGACY : Former House Speaker Dennis Hastert (R-Ill.), the longest-serving Republican Speaker in the chamber’s history who became one of the highest-ranking U.S. officials to ever serve time in prison, has died at age 84 .

He died Saturday of “natural causes,” a county coroner revealed Monday.

Hastert served as Speaker from 1999, taking over for Rep. Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.), until 2007, when Democrats reclaimed control of the House, as part of a congressional career that spanned two decades. He played a key role throughout much of George W. Bush ‘s presidency, helping usher through two rounds of major tax cuts.

But his legacy was overshadowed by revelations that he paid hush money to a man who alleged Hastert sexually abused him when the future congressman was a high school wrestling coach decades earlier. An investigation was launched into allegations that Hastert abused at least four boys at the school.

The statute of limitations concerning the abuse allegations had long since expired, but Hastert pleaded guilty to financial crimes related to his conduct, leading to a 15-month prison sentence.

The president and first lady will participate in a gold star families reception at 1 p.m. He will travel to Baltimore to deliver remarks at the Sparrows Point Shipyard at 4 p.m. and then return to the White House.

The Senate will meet at 1:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

The House will convene at 4 p.m. for a pro forma session.

GLOVES COME OFF: An increasingly personal clash between Vice President Vance and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) has been playing out in recent days, offering an early glimpse of what the 2028 GOP presidential primary might look after the midterms, The Hill’s Amie Parnes reports .

The vice president took aim at Cruz last week, saying it was “really obvious” that the Texas Republican planned to run for president in 2028.

Cruz shot back in an interview with Politico over the weekend, saying, “ In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure.”

“So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes,” Cruz added.

Vance, as vice president, finds himself in a tricky position, having to navigate the administration’s poor approval ratings while building support within Trump’s MAGA base. Much of the early discussion about the 2028 GOP primary has focused on a potential contest between Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to be Trump’s heir apparent.

“Vance should be insecure because of Donald Trump’s poll numbers, and the fact that, at this point, Trump isn’t even willing to commit to his vice president is very telling,” Republican strategist Susan Del Percio , who does not support the president, told Parnes.

As vice president, Vance cannot distance himself from the administration’s policies, but the latest feud with Cruz could be an opportunity for the senator, who “has found his moment to play on a no-win situation for JD Vance,” Del Percio said.

“If you’re Cruz, it’s just good politics,” s he added. “He’s found a weak spot and he’s not letting go.”

PLAGUE SCARE : The State Department said it’s monitoring the status of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia in the aftermath of the death of a lab worker.

The woman in her late 20s reportedly worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, located in the Irkutsk Oblast in Russia. She was reported to have died from pneumonia of unknown origin.

More than 200 people are under medical observation in the area.

Russian authorities haven’t confirmed the cause of the worker’s death, but reports have indicated it may be pneumonic plague, a disease caused by the same bacteria that led to the Black Death of the 1300s. The bubonic plague is more common, though the pneumonic plague is considered much more serious.

The State Department told NewsNation that it’s aware of the suspected outbreak and is closely monitoring the situation, along with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other agencies.

“Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly,” an official said. “Plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early. Cases occur naturally in many parts of the world.”

Pneumonic plague can cause symptoms within one to four days after exposure that include weakness, headache, fever, chills, body aches, nausea and shortness of breath. If left untreated, the disease is almost always fatal, though it can be treated with widely available antibiotics.

Starting the antibiotics within 24 hours of symptoms appearing gives the best chance for survival. The disease can be spread through respiratory droplets from infected animals or people.

Trump weighed in on the outbreak Monday, saying he’s concerned and that the U.S. would help Russia with the suspected outbreak.

And finally … Vanity Fair referred to Vance as the “MAGA heir” and Rubio as the “MAGA spare” in its “New Establishment” list Monday.

The list included several Trump administration officials and other top lawmakers, such as California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), and Big Tech leaders, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk .

The magazine described the strengths and appeal of both Vance and Rubio as part of the 2028 presidential conversation while acknowledging their potential vulnerabilities. The list is made up of 50 people or groups who have “defined the moment,” referring to figures who should “inspire complicated feelings.”

Others in the president’s orbit include his children, Donald Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump , and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner .

articles.title: Provide time, order and mercy for Salvadoran TPS holders
articles.summary: I understand that Temporary Protected Status was never intended as a permanent immigration status. But I ask that the administration extend it for Salvadorans so they have sufficient time to pursue other lawful alternatives and prepare responsibly for what may come.
articles.body:
I write as a proud U.S. citizen, but also as someone who has experienced firsthand the trauma and uncertainty of being an immigrant and, later, the relief and opportunity afforded by Temporary Protected Status before I obtained permanent residency.

I came to the U.S. as a young man, fleeing the civil war in El Salvador and seeking safety and the opportunity for a better life. Through the Temporary Protected Status program, I received authorization to work and was able to remain legally in the U.S. That work permit allowed me to hold different jobs, support myself, and pay taxes. I worked mostly in the construction and the janitorial industries — jobs which gave me a profound sense of dignity. They allowed me not only to earn an honest living, but also to know that, through my work, service, and taxes, I was contributing to the country that had opened its doors to me.

In time, other doors opened. I entered formation for the priesthood and was ordained in 2004. In 2023, I was ordained an auxiliary bishop of Washington, and since Jul. 2, I have had the privilege of serving as Bishop of the Diocese of Wheeling-Charleston, which encompasses the entire state of West Virginia.

I share these details because my experience has taught me what legal status and the opportunity to work can mean in the life of an immigrant. What the Salvadoran community in the U.S. is facing today, with an uncertain future, could have been my story.

I understand both the love that immigrants can have for this nation and the personal struggles of Salvadoran families living in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status. As a priest and bishop, I have walked with this community for many years. And in recent months, I have witnessed their fear, anxiety and uncertainty about their future that I have not seen in many years: the fear that decades of lawful life in this country may end not gradually, but suddenly.

Salvadorans are among the most deeply rooted Temporary Protected Status holders in the U.S. Over the years, they have built careers, purchased homes, started businesses, raised families, and contributed to the communities in which they live. Many are parents of U.S. citizen children.

Ending their status abruptly would therefore affect far more than the holders themselves. It would affect American families, workplaces, parishes, neighborhoods, and local economies. Industries such as construction, hospitality, agriculture, nursing, childcare, and elder care could lose hardworking men and women on whom they have relied for many years.

I do not write as a political actor, nor do I dispute the right and responsibility of this nation to order its borders and enforce its laws. That right is not in question, and the Church has never taught otherwise. I write as a bishop who has walked with this particular community and who asks the administration, with the respect due its office, to grant an extension of Temporary Protected Status for Salvadorans so that they — and the families and employers that depend upon them — have sufficient time to pursue other lawful alternatives and prepare responsibly for what may come.

I understand that Temporary Protected Status was never intended to become a permanent immigration status. Yet for many Salvadorans, it has remained a lifeline for decades. During that time, these men and women and their families have been woven into the fabric of this country.

I ask, therefore, for time: an extended period of transition for Salvadorans before any change of status takes effect. Such a transition would allow families to prepare rather than face sudden separation or removal. It would give employers time to adjust without unnecessary disruption. It would also give El Salvador, my country of birth, time to prepare responsibly to receive those who may eventually return.

El Salvador has made significant progress in recent years, particularly in improving public safety. That progress should be acknowledged and encouraged. At the same time, receiving large numbers of people presently employed and established in the U.S. would present serious economic and social challenges.

Salvadorans working in this country contribute to the U.S. economy through their labor and taxes, often while also supporting families and communities in El Salvador through remittances.

Most importantly, additional time would allow Congress the opportunity to do what ultimately only Congress can: consider and enact a permanent, lawful solution for people who have lived, worked, paid taxes, raised families, and contributed to this nation for decades.

I respectfully urge an extension of Temporary Protected Status and a compassionate, orderly transition for the sons and daughters of El Salvador.

Evelio Menjivar-Ayala, a native of El Salvador, is the tenth bishop of the Catholic Diocese of Wheeling-Charleston, which covers the state of West Virginia.

articles.title: Iran is losing — that’s why we should expect and prepare for more terrorist attacks
articles.summary: Two recent terrorist incidents, both fortunately unsuccessful, may provide a partial insight into a larger, longer-term Iranian strategy.
articles.body:
Contrary to the picture conveyed by some U.S. media, Iran’s regime is not doing well in its ongoing war against America and Israel. Damage to its nuclear-weapons program, air defenses, and military-industrial complex is significant. Its economy, already in wretched shape before the war, has deteriorated further because of the U.S. naval blockade. Gulf Arab oil exports are rebounding because Tehran has failed to close the Strait of Hormuz and hold the global economy hostage .

American successes, however, do not mean Iran’s regime is defeated, much less overthrown, which should be Washington’s objective. Instead, surviving elements of its badly fractured regime may well be turning away from conventional military operations — a losing game for the regime, perhaps — and instead toward terrorism and other forms of asymmetric warfare.

Lower-profile and somewhat deniable acts of terrorism, undertaken away from the battlefield, could sap U.S. resolve and give Tehran time to recover from the initial American-Israeli bombings.

Two recent terrorist incidents, both fortunately unsuccessful, may provide a partial insight into a larger, longer-term Iranian strategy.

The United Kingdom’s Royal Air Force base at Fairford, England, is far from Iran, but not far enough to keep Iranian-backed terrorists away. Specifics are still emerging about what appears to be a thwarted attack on RAF Fairford, whose facilities are critical to US Air Force operations in Europe and the Middle East and especially in Washington’s attacks against Iran’s nuclear program and military-industrial complex.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said publicly there are “strong indications” Iran was involved. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that his government had supplied Britain intelligence about possible Iranian threats just before London foiled the potential attack.

Terrorist attacks in Great Britain by the Provisional Irish Republican Army in the 1960s and 1970s led to significant efforts, especially in London, to make bombings and other attacks more difficult. After 9/11, as in the U.S., more security steps were taken, but vulnerabilities remained.

In 2018, Russian agents poisoned the Russian exile Sergei Skripal and his daughter, but they were treated and survived. Tehran has long posed threats to regime opponents among diaspora Iranians, with more than 20 mortal threats reported since 1922. The Jewish community IN THE U.K. remains under Iranian terrorist assault .

There is, as yet, no evidence of Iranian involvement in the attempted hijacking of FlyDubai 1073 by its co-pilot, Omani citizen Hamam al-Hammami. Nonetheless, the government of Oman, a Muslim Arab nation, considered his views sufficiently extremist to bar him from flying for the state airline . Why FlyDubai later hired al-Hammami, and why he was assigned to co-pilot flight 1073 are still not publicly known.

Even if Hammami is actually a “lone wolf” terrorist, radicalized and operating on his own, he has brought the reality of suicidal aircraft hijackings back to center stage globally. Notwithstanding the countless safety improvements made since 9/11, this Islamicist found a hole in air travel’s defenses , and nearly murdered 182 passengers and crew. Using the “crash ax” stored in cockpits for use in emergencies, Hammami severely wounded the pilot and seized the airplane’s controls . It is not yet known whether he intended to crash the plane in the desert or strike a building in Israel, al Qaeda-style.

Although we are still operating with incomplete information about both Fairford and FlyDubai, we know enough to take corrective actions, particularly against other potential Iranian threats.

The fact of Fairford’s role in the war against Iran weighs heavily in favor of Iranian involvement. The U.S. and Israel should be concerned about further attacks on military, diplomatic or even private, commercial targets at home and overseas, and considering and implementing enhanced safety precautions. Iranian assassination attempts in the U.S. against President Trump and others, in retaliation for U.S. elimination of Quds Force leader Qassem Soleimani, have already occurred. More such attempts are likely, given the current war.

Iran may have had no involvement, even indirectly, with FlyDubai 1073. But the publicity attendant to the attack could well inspire others, quite apart from Iran. Accordingly, American and international civil aviation authorities should not simply brush aside the specter of more 9/11-style hijackings by “copycats,” or even Iran itself getting into the act if it wasn’t already.

With FlyDubai as the impetus, considerably greater attention should be given to what could pose dangers on the air-side of airports, after security, not just on the public-facing land-side. Screening passengers and cargo entering airports was not FlyDubai’s problem, although that scrutiny should hardly be lessened. Instead, the potential threat arises from the workaday demands of running a complex transportation business largely out of public view, what it involves and who has access to it.

We treat Fairford and FlyDubai as mere isolated incidents at our own peril. We have been warned. We should move rapidly now, with Israel and other allies, to guard against more terrorist attacks.

John Bolton was national security adviser to President Trump from 2018 to 2019 and U.S. ambassador to the United Nations from 2005 to 2006. He held senior State Department posts at times between 1981 and 2005.

articles.title: Trump approval rating mired at record low: Poll
articles.summary: President Trump maintained his record low approval rating in a new survey released Monday, as Republicans push to ramp up support for their party’s candidates with around four weeks until the midterms. The Reuters/Ipsos poll found the president’s approval held steady at the 32 percent rating from the polling center’s survey last month. Trump’s waning…
articles.body:
President Trump maintained his record low approval rating in a new survey released Monday, as Republicans push to ramp up support for their party’s candidates with around four weeks until the midterms.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll found the president’s approval held steady at the 32 percent rating from the polling center’s survey last month.

Trump’s waning support has cast a dark shadow over the GOP’s prospects this November, as he continues to urge voters to pretend he is “ on the ballot ” in this election.

During Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas last month, the president promised every American adult $5,000 dividend checks if the party keeps control of both chambers of Congress next year.

Among registered voters surveyed, 44 percent said they preferred Democrats over the 37 percent who backed Republicans. Independent voters also favored Democratic candidates, with 37 percent choosing the part compared to 21 percent who supported the GOP, according to the poll.

Additionally, the data shows Republicans lost ground among Hispanic voters from the last time the pollster surveyed respondents on this question. This voting bloc was key to Trump’s victory in the 2024 presidential election, but his support from this demographic has taken a hit amid his administration’s mass deportation operations.

Only 24 percent of Hispanic voters in the new survey said they approved of the president’s job performance. Additionally, 26 percent of these voters said they would support their GOP candidate in the midterm elections.

Another 52 percent of respondents said they would back a Democrat — up from the 46 percent who supported Democrats in an August poll.

A separate poll from NBC News and Telemundo showed a similar change within this voting demographic, with 59 percent preferring Democrats to win in November compared to 35 percent who favored Republicans.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey was conducted among 4,506 U.S. adults from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5. It has a margin of error of approximately 2 percentage points.
