articles.title: Are ‘tradwives’ relevant now in conservative movement?
articles.summary: Two years ago, the conservative movement seemed captivated by the ideal of the “tradwife” — a rejection of modern feminist thinking and an embrace of traditional roles for men and women, where the woman stays at home taking care of the children, cooking and managing the house while her husband works. This new standard showed…
articles.body:
Two years ago, the conservative movement seemed captivated by the ideal of the “tradwife” — a rejection of modern feminist thinking and an embrace of traditional roles for men and women, where the woman stays at home taking care of the children, cooking and managing the house while her husband works. This new standard showed up in politics, too, such as when Republican Sen. Katie Britt (Ala.) filmed the rebuttal to then- President Biden ‘s final State of the Union from her kitchen, appearing more like a soccer mom than a senator.

But as President Trump ‘s coalition has shifted, some conservative women who tried the tradwife life, seeking influence and online fame, have burned out . More broadly, the conservative vision of the ideal housewife is not widespread enough to make for policy bolstering it, as evidenced by the all-out firestorm online over a White House proposal to pay stay-at-home parents.

At the same time, podcasters who preach the Christian “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) mom gospel — like Allie Beth Stuckey and Alex Clark — still top the charts in their respective categories. Prominent GOP women, like former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt , have stepped back from full-time work to focus on raising children. Katie Miller , a popular conservative podcaster whose husband Stephen Miller is White House deputy chief of staff, was one of many online to trumpet the results of a sketchy survey earlier this year that suggested a majority of Generation Z women wanted to be married with children and have their husband as the top earner.

“The biggest lie women were told is that success comes from the workplace,” said Miller, who recently gave birth to her fourth child. “Success is expanding humanity for its survival. The joy of motherhood is indescribable and better than any job title.”

So, which is it? For some family policy experts and those who track such trends, there does seem to be a shift away from the tradwife in how conservative women, in particular, are viewing their ideal role. While baking sourdough every day, wearing dresses to work in the garden and homeschooling children form a rosy aesthetic for an Instagram page, conservatives’ interests in reviving traditional housewife and motherhood roles has yet to translate into political reality — even after nearly two years of control in Washington.

One explanation is that the tradwife remains nebulous and mostly aspirational. Hadley Heath Manning , a senior fellow at the Independent Women’s Forum who writes about family policy and gender issues, said there’s a gap between some more appealing tenets of the tradwife aesthetic — like spending more time with the kids, having time to keep a tidy home and embracing femininity — and the underlying philosophical extreme some advocates want, which includes submission to one’s husband.

“Anything is more fun when it’s just a pop culture trend, and when it becomes politicized, gets less fun,” Manning said. “There’s a fascination with it, but if you dig into the polling about what they want, it doesn’t really align with the strictest or most conservative view of a traditional wife.”

That gap also demonstrably cleaves young women from their male peers. In a 29-country survey by King’s College London earlier this year, 31 percent of Gen Z men agreed that “a wife should always obey her husband,” against 18 percent of Gen Z women. That’s an increase from baby boomer men, 13 percent of whom agreed (compared to 6 percent of baby boomer women).

Brad Wilcox , senior fellow at the Institute for Family Studies and professor at the University of Virginia , is one of the leading academic experts on marriage and family life. He said that while data reflects an increased interest from young conservative men and women in the tradwife ideal, the men seem to have internalized it even more as a reaction against social change.

“This is particularly salient for conservative younger men who I think both look at the broader culture as having moved too far to the left and also kind of feel like men’s status is eroding their pathways to providing,” Wilcox said. “Marriage and family life are becoming more precarious, more difficult, and they’re looking for a cultural turn to the older ways of family life to lock in their position and place in American life and the American family more particularly.”

Many of those men voted for Trump and Republicans in 2024 for similar reasons. But there’s a political downside to marrying the tradwife movement to the GOP: It has created an easy attack lane from the left. After Britt’s State of the Union response, liberal commentators panned her approach as fitting in with a Republican goal to diminish women.

“It’s no accident that Alabama Sen. Katie Britt issued the Republican Party’s response to the State of the Union address from her kitchen table, since the kitchen is precisely where the GOP would prefer we women spend most of our lives,” freelance writer Andrea Grimes wrote at the time , in chorus with others .

That’s not a surprising connection to make, Manning said.

“Without a real clear definition of what a tradwife is, it becomes easy to say, ‘Oh, they want every woman to be a tradwife, they want to go backwards in time, they’re nostalgic for the time before the 19th Amendment or time before women had equal rights,’” Manning said of those on the political left vis-a-vis the right. “And that’s certainly not the mainstream position of the Republican Party or, you know, any major group that I know of on the right.”

Conservative women and men alike acknowledge the good that the tradwife set of values becoming more mainstream has done for the cause. Erika Bachiochi, legal scholar and fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center , said the online tradwife movement has helped bring some tenets of family values into focus for the better, even though the “staged” aesthetic is not itself worth pursuing.

“I’ll be very happy for the online right to move beyond applauding the commercialized performativity of the tradwife phenomenon, even as it has brought welcome attention to the long-ignored goods of the home,” Bachiochi said. “For women and men to cultivate the virtues needed for a happy family life, they need models and mentors in real life, not staged images on the screen.”

Manning also said the tradwife trend glamorized the success of the married-parent model for raising children, itself a proven sociological reality .

“I do think the recognition of what social science says about what’s best for families and what’s best for children has always been the same,” she said. “It’s best for children to be in a family with a married mom and dad, to be in the same household with a married mom and dad. That’s never changed. And so the tradwife thing did put more of a, you know, online sexy hashtag around that.”

Despite the fervor for aspects of the tradwife life, even close to the centers of power, mainstream Republican politics has been slow to cement any of these ideas into policy. Wilcox said that comes from the generational gap — most politicians are still millennials, Generation X or boomers, who grew up in an age of feminism that cut across both parties, while their younger, very online staffers are the ones looking ahead to a future restoration of traditional gender roles, spurred on by the influencer class.

“It’s certainly the case when you talk to staffers on the Hill on the Republican side, their support for, you know, kind of a more conservative cultural agenda, like around reviving the male breadwinner model, is much more common now than it would have been, I would say 15 years ago,” Wilcox said. “But again, we’re talking about a generational difference, and they’re not the senator, they’re not the congressman or congresswoman, but they’re, you know, the next generation, so to speak.”

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments, and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

CONSERVATIVES BALK AT HUCKABEE SANDERS’ WORK REQUIREMENTS AD

The latest flash point for the online conservative civil war is a video of a guy playing video games and eating snacks.

It’s an advertisement from Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), who is running for reelection this year. The video depicts a young, frumpy-looking man playing video games from a beanbag chair while covered in Cheeto-like snacks. Sanders, as the camera cuts to her, introduces him as “ Brad ,” who has “made relaxing into a full-time profession.”

The ad goes on to trumpet the new Medicaid work requirements, which the state is rolling out as part of Medicaid changes Congress passed in the reconciliation bill last year. About 20 percent of Arkansas’s Medicaid recipients are expected to lose coverage next year due to the work requirements.

But the controversy over the ad was not really about the underlying policy, which conservatives generally love. The use of a young white man as the poster child for undeserved welfare quickly stoked online fervor, with critics arguing it unfairly “demonized” white men — the core of the Trump voting coalition.

“The backbone of the 2024 coalition that President Trump, Charlie Kirk , and so many others worked tirelessly to build was young white men,” wrote Jack Posobiec , a right-wing media anchor and conspiracy theorist. “Why is the GOP now demonizing them a month before the election?”

An account linked to Steve Bannon ’s podcast, “Bannon’s War Room,” posted a video of the ad and linked it to the GOP message going into the 2026 elections.

“With young men already checking out of the GOP, this is who Republicans decided to make the problem,” the post read.

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) also joined the fray.

“Sarah Huckabee Sanders doubles down on young, white, male, gamers as the face of welfare fraud,” Mace wrote in response to Sanders’s post. “And she gets roasted for it.”

While the criticism is somewhat based in political reality on a national level —recent polling shows young men are warming back up to Democrats over Republicans — in Arkansas, Sanders’s appeal isn’t unfounded.

Kevin Corinth , in an analysis of census data for the Center for Opportunity and Social Mobility at the American Enterprise Institute , ran the numbers and found that a majority — 61 percent — of those expected to be affected by the new work requirements are white.

“The ad’s loudest critics object to the depiction of Brad as a white man. Some believe a woman and especially a black person would have been a more realistic choice for the ad’s protagonist,” Corinth wrote. “In reality, there are far more white people than black people among the population subject to the state’s Medicaid work requirement, and while women outnumber men the difference is modest.”

articles.title: Return of split-ticket voting could hurt Republicans
articles.summary: A resurgence of split-ticket voting may occur in upcoming midterm elections due to Donald Trump’s popularity among certain GOP voters and specific local race dynamics in states like Texas and Iowa.
articles.body:
There was a time decades ago when voters often engaged in split-ticket voting. That is, electing a Democratic candidate running statewide for one office — such as for president, governor or U.S. Senate — while electing a Republican for a different office. In recent elections, that practice had largely disappeared. But with the Trump-led Republicans doing so poorly in the polls , we may see a resurgence of the split-ticket voter in November.

Split-ticket voting used to be fairly common. What Ballotpedia calls “mixed-party election outcomes” rose from a low in 1920 to its peak in 1984, when 58.4 percent of voters would vote for both a Republican and a Democrat in federal and state elections. That practice fell to a historic low by 2016. In that year, no state elected a senator from one party while voting for the presidential candidate from the other party.

Just before the 2020 election, the Pew Research Center noted , “In an era of increasing partisanship, split-ticket voting continues to be rare in U.S. politics.” In that presidential election year, Pew claimed that only 4 percent of registered voters in states with a Senate election said they would be voting for a different party candidate for president and the Senate.

But split-ticket voting increased in 2024. According to Pew , voters in four states that voted for President Trump also elected a Democratic senator. Pew concludes, “That may not seem like a lot, but it’s twice as many ‘mismatches’ between states’ presidential and U.S. Senate results as in all Senate elections held in 2020, 2021 and 2022 combined.”

While Trump isn’t on the ticket in the coming midterm election, we may see an even bigger increase in split-ticket voting, helping Democrats running in statewide races in red states.

For example, in Texas, the Democratic candidate for Senate, state Rep. James Talarico (D), has led Republican candidate Attorney General Ken Paxton in the polls for weeks, usually by between 2 and 5 points.

In contrast, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has led his Democratic challenger, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, in most, but not all, polls — usually by between 2 and 5 points .

Could very red Texas elect a Democratic senator and Republican governor? The polls indicate it’s possible.

And then there is Iowa, which has been voting red for several election cycles. As it stands, the Democratic candidate for governor, state auditor Rob Sand, has been polling consistently stronger than the Republican candidate, Zach Lahn. However, polling for the Republican candidate for Iowa’s open Senate seat, Rep. Ashley Hinson (R), has been mixed against her Democratic opponent, state Rep. Josh Turek. So, at this point it’s quite possible that Iowa could elect a Democratic governor and a Republican senator.

Or consider Maine. The Democratic candidate for governor, former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree, is polling way ahead of the Republican candidate, Bobby Charles, and has been for weeks. The incumbent Senate candidate, Susan Collins (R), has a small lead in some polls against her Democratic challenger, former state Sen. Troy Jackson (D), although she trails in others. However, in 2020, Collins was the one Senate candidate in the country who won in a state that voted for the presidential candidate from the other party, Joe Biden. If Collins does that again, it will be an indication of Mainers voting split-ticket.

There are several other states where there could be a senator/governor split ticket — Alaska, Ohio, Georgia, New Hampshire and Kansas, and possibly more.

The problem for Republicans is that most of these potential split-ticket races appear to be in red states where a Republican ends up on the short end of the ticket-splitting. Indeed, both the Cook Political Report and Larry Sabato’s Center for Politics at the University of Virginia have recently made multiple rating changes for the midterm election, virtually all in favor of Democrats .

Split-ticket voting began to decline in the 1990s and 2000s, as both parties became more ideologically committed. Today, voters who align with either political party are generally reluctant to vote for candidates from the other. But Trump’s polarizing actions and comments, low approval ratings on the economy and inflation, and the war with Iran are pushing voters — especially independents but even many traditional Republicans — to reconsider their split-ticket reluctance.

Even longtime Republican strategist Karl Rove has announced he will be a split-ticket voter, voting for one Democratic candidate in Texas (for railroad commissioner) because of some very controversial remarks made by the Republican candidate.

If we see a return of split-ticket voting, or even worse for Republicans, a blue wave, Republicans will have no one to blame but themselves. They have followed Trump in abandoning long-held Republican principles on fiscal responsibility, limited government, and Congress’s constitutional role in declaring war and imposing taxes (tariffs).

When voters split their tickets in the 1980s, they were voting for candidates in both parties. In the coming midterm election, they won’t be voting for Democrats so much as voting against Republicans.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.

articles.title: Jack Smith did not deserve the Senate trashing
articles.summary: Smith’s questioning before the Senate was a monument to unfairness.
articles.body:
I am critical of Jack Smith, the former special counsel, who failed to convict President Trump for trying to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election and for mishandling classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate after he left office.

In failing to bring Trump to book, Smith failed in his prosecutor’s obligation to see that justice is done. But Smith is neither perjurer nor “ villain ” nor “ dirtbag ,” as Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) savaged him last week before the Senate Judiciary Committee.

Smith delayed indicting Trump over the events of Jan. 6, not getting around to it until August 2023 , over a year after he was appointed. He also brought the documents case in Florida instead of Washington and consequently drew an inexperienced judge in the tank for Trump. As a consequence, neither case went anywhere.

Smith was appointed in November 2022 , three days after Trump announced he was running for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination. Attorney General Merrick Garland, who could have indicted Trump in 2021, said in a statement that since both Trump and Biden were likely to be presidential candidates, Smith’s appointment was meant to underscore the Department’s commitment to “make decisions indisputably guided only by the facts and the law.”

Trump, following the Roy Cohn playbook of lashing out at his accusers, immediately called Smith “ a political hit man .”

In our antiquated constitutional architecture, it is virtually impossible to investigate a high-ranking political figure of the party out of power without the appearance of partisanship. The only guardrails are our grand juries and independent judiciary.

On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court after delaying matters for more than three months, largely agreed with Trump on the Jan. 6 case . They stripped the case of any conduct that could fall under “official duties.” Another grand jury returned an indictment for the same offenses. But after Trump was reelected, Smith had to dismiss both cases because of the longstanding position of the Department of Justice that sitting presidents cannot be prosecuted.

The cases may be resumed once Trump is no longer president, unless he complicates matters by pardoning himself on the way out, which he is likely to do.

Smith’s questioning before the Senate was a monument to unfairness. He was under oath, and his Republican tormentors were protected by constitutional privilege . They could smear him with any lie they might devise. Last week, focusing on Trump’s Jan. 6 indictment , the MAGA senators were unbridled in their efforts to heap Smith with abuse.

Schmitt, touted as a potential 2028 vice presidential candidate if JD Vance gets the nod for the top spot, was the deputized hit man to shoot down Smith as a lying out-of-control partisan who was part of a conspiracy with Fulton County, Georgia District Attorney Fani Willis and her lover/colleague Nathan Wade to get Trump.

But it turns out that Schmitt was shooting airballs.

Schmitt asked Smith: “Did you go to an NBA game between the Golden State Warriors and the Atlanta Hawks on Feb. 3, 2024?”

Smith answered : “I really don’t think so. It’s possible I flew through the Atlanta airport on the way to Florida, but I do not have a recollection of going to Atlanta. I definitely did not go to a Hawks game. I’m sure of that.”

“Did you ever meet Nathan Wade or Fani Willis in your time as special counsel,” Schmitt asked . “No,” said Smith.

Then Schmitt sprang what proved to be a non-trap: “What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warrior-Hawks game on February 3, 2024, the day after Willis and Wade announced their affair?” A staffer and Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) briefly flashed a poster board.

Smith said : “You just took it down really quick. If I could look at that again?” Schmitt declined and accused Smith of perjury. No judge would allow any lawyer to engage in such chicanery.

Smith said : “I recall going to a University of Maryland basketball game where Caitlin Clark was playing right around that time…. You could check if that was the exact date. It was Maryland playing Iowa, I think, February of 2024.”

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) rode to the rescue. In truth and in fact, Smith was in Maryland, where the University of Maryland’s Terrapins played the University of Iowa Hawkeyes.

Klobuchar utterly destroyed Schmitt: “You had teams wrong, sir.”

Schmitt exploded, accusing Klobuchar of “trying to rehabilitate the witness.” But rehabilitating a witness is a perfectly legitimate technique lawyers use to protect the record. Tapes of the games found Smith in the stands at the Maryland game .

Smith stood firm : “Our investigation proved beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in serious crimes against our nation. If asked whether to prosecute a former president today, based on the same facts, I would do so regardless of whether that president was a Republican or a Democrat.”

If one were to fault Smith, it would be for failing to close the deal.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: Newsom rips Trump for saying Iran can ‘take out’ LA and San Diego
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) slammed President Trump as “deranged and dangerous” after he suggested Iran could “take out” two major U.S. cities located in the Golden State if the country developed a nuclear weapon. Trump made the comment during remarks at a political rally in Grand Island, Neb., on Monday, in which he defended…
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) slammed President Trump as “ deranged and dangerous ” after he suggested Iran could “take out” two major U.S. cities located in the Golden State if the country developed a nuclear weapon.

Trump made the comment during remarks at a political rally in Grand Island, Neb., on Monday, in which he defended his administration’s military operations against Iran despite rising costs for U.S. consumers amid the conflict.

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe,” the president said, before adding that Tehran could “take out a city.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“Let ‘em take out Los Angeles, let ‘em take out San Diego,” he continued. “This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”

Newsom, who is weighing a presidential run in 2028, accused Trump of encouraging attacks on these two California cities.

“After sending the National Guard to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” the governor wrote in a social media post . “He is deranged and dangerous.”

In a Tuesday statement, White House communications director Steven Cheung disputed this characterization of the president’s remarks.

“The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” Cheung wrote on social media .

“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” he continued. “America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”

Other California officials joined the governor in denouncing the remarks.

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria (D) wrote in a social media post that his city was “not collateral damage.”

“We are not expendable,” Gloria added. “And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) also condemned the president’s comments.

“His statements against our city are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety,” Bass wrote on social platform X .

“The role of the president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” she continued. “In the face of irresponsible threats, as Angelenos, we know how to stand together and protect our city.”

articles.title: How Americans helped create the Chinese car tech capable of 'spying'
articles.summary: University of Wisconsin-Madison researchers worked on China's vehicle-road-cloud technology that lets roadside cameras track and command vehicles.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison overlapped on work with China's powerful police ministry developing vehicle technology capable of tracking cars and overtaking driving functions, according to findings from a report shared exclusively with Fox News Digital ahead of its release. Beijing has already begun deploying the systems across China. The technology, known as "vehicle-road-cloud" integration, links cars with roadside cameras and sensors and centralized cloud platforms, allowing authorities to monitor traffic in real time and, at its most advanced levels, send commands to connected vehicles. The implications of connected vehicles have alarmed U.S. officials. The Commerce Department moved last year to restrict certain Chinese and Russian connected-vehicle technology in the United States, warning that foreign adversaries could potentially collect sensitive information about American drivers or remotely manipulate their cars. HARVARD, NYU AMONG 30 UNIVERSITIES HIT WITH PENTAGON FOREIGN-TIE AUDIT DEADLINE In 2016, then-UW Vice Provost Jeffrey Russell traveled to Southeast University, where the schools signed agreements covering research, faculty exchanges, student training and plans to create a joint institute. The following year, Southeast University's president traveled to Madison to formally establish the Joint Research Institute, according to university records cited by Strategy Risks. The institute focused on intelligent transportation, connected and autonomous vehicles and vehicle-road-cloud technology. UW-Madison's own College of Engineering wrote in 2019 that the institute had "launched in late 2017." Two years later, UW researchers appeared on technical work that also involved an institute of China's Ministry of Public Security. Five UW-Madison researchers were among 46 contributors to a Chinese industry report on vehicle-road cooperative automated driving, according to Strategy Risks. The UW-SEU joint institute was listed first among the report's drafting units, while the Traffic Management Research Institute of China's Ministry of Public Security was listed seventh. The extent of UW-Madison's institutional involvement in the joint institute is disputed. Counsel for a UW professor told Strategy Risks that the contemplated arrangement was never implemented and that the institute was never operational, funded or staffed by UW. Strategy Risks said it has not independently resolved that dispute, pointing to public records from both universities describing the institute as established. UW-Madison did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Related vehicle-road-cloud technology was, meanwhile, becoming part of China's national connected-vehicle push. In 2023, three major Chinese transportation and communications standards bodies published a framework for vehicle-road-cloud integration. Southeast University was among the drafters alongside the Road Traffic Safety Research Center of China's Ministry of Public Security. The following year, the MPS joined four other Chinese ministries in launching a vehicle-road-cloud pilot program across 20 cities and regional groupings. OHIO STATE PAYS $2.1M SETTLEMENT AS IT ADMITS RESEARCHER HAD ‘INAPPROPRIATE FOREIGN AFFILIATIONS’ TO CHINA Under the government plan, participating cities are to install connected roadside equipment and sensing systems and build city-level cloud platforms capable of communicating with vehicles. The platforms can provide information to vehicles and assist with decision-making, planning and control, while safety-monitoring systems track participating vehicles in real time. Chinese authorities describe the program as an effort to improve traffic safety, advance autonomous driving and accelerate the country's connected-vehicle industry. But those same capabilities have raised security concerns in Washington, where officials have warned that connected-vehicle systems could be exploited to collect sensitive data or remotely manipulate vehicles. Strategy Risks stressed that it is not accusing UW-Madison of intentionally transferring technology to China's security apparatus. "Strategy Risks does not allege that UW-Madison, either on its own or through the JRI, deliberately channeled U.S. technology into Chinese surveillance or military systems," the report states. But the group argues the research nevertheless contributed to technology that later took on broader applications in China. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The available evidence indicates that research conducted by scholars affiliated with the JRI contributed to the development of a civilian-framed dual-use technology in technical areas that also received U.S. institutional and federal research support," the report states. "When Beijing incorporated this technology into national standards, the state absorbed a system that has significant surveillance, military, and human rights dimensions."

articles.title: Remote employees need better management, not more surveillance
articles.summary: Slack lights up at 9:07 a.m. with a two-line message from a manager: “Let’s tighten the plan. Circle back today.” In a home office, that can read like a fire drill.
articles.body:
Slack lights up at 9:07 a.m. with a two-line message from a manager: “Let’s tighten the plan. Circle back today.” In a home office, that can read like a fire drill. In an office, the same ambiguity may get resolved with a hallway question, a whiteboard sketch, or a quick clarification. Remote and hybrid work put more pressure on managers to make expectations explicit.

Flexible work has become a durable part of the labor market. According to a recent Gallup report , 52 percent of U.S. employees with remote-capable jobs work hybrid and 26 percent work fully remote. And employees place substantial value on flexibility. A 2025 National Bureau of Economic Research study of U.S. tech workers estimated that workers would accept an average 25 percent pay cut for partly or fully remote roles.

Pew Research Center likewise found that most hybrid workers prefer to remain hybrid , while many workers who rarely or never work from home would choose at least some remote work if they could.

But a Founder Reports survey of 1,000 U.S. remote and hybrid employees shows where managers still fall short: Eighty-five percent of respondents said clear communication from managers matters, but only 51 percent said their manager provides it. Just 40 percent said they receive clear feedback.

The problem is easy to recognize: When people cannot rely on proximity for context, vague direction becomes expensive. That does not mean every job should be remote, of course, or that location never matters. It means leaders should stop treating attendance as a substitute for management.

The practical response starts with written clarity. Managers should put goals, decision owners, deadlines, and definitions of “done” in shared documents rather than leaving them scattered across meetings and chat. This does not require turning every decision into bureaucracy; it requires making important context durable enough that employees do not have to reconstruct it from memory or guess what a manager means.

Managers also need response rules. Employees should know which channel fits an urgent issue, when silence means “keep going,” when a decision needs escalation, and how quickly a manager will respond. Those rules prevent routine uncertainty from becoming a stream of pings while still giving employees a clear path when work truly gets stuck.

Feedback needs the same discipline. Gallup’s updated research on manager feedback reports that 80 percent of employees who received meaningful feedback in the previous week were fully engaged, regardless of where they worked. A weekly check-in can therefore stay short: confirm priorities and surface blockers, discuss one recent example, and agree on the next action. Remember: the value comes from consistency and specificity, not from adding another long meeting.

Managers should also separate accountability from surveillance. Remote employees need clear standards, but constant status checking often signals that the standards themselves are weak. When a manager defines the output, the deadline, the decision rights, and the escalation path, employees can act with more autonomy while the manager retains visibility into whether the work is moving.

It is essential that managers of hybrid teams are able to distinguish coordination from mere presence. Some work benefits from people being together at the same time, whether in a room or on a call. Other work improves when employees can focus independently. The manager’s job is to identify which tasks require synchronous collaboration; schedule that coordination deliberately, then leave the rest of the week open for execution. This approach gives office time a purpose instead of turning attendance itself into the purpose.

The best evidence for hybrid work points in the same direction. A Stanford-led randomized experiment at Trip.com found that employees working from home two days a week quit at a 33 percent lower rate while productivity and promotion rates held steady . That result came from a structured hybrid arrangement, not from abandoning coordination. Flexibility worked because the organization paired it with a workable system.

Leaders deciding where people should work need to consider the job, the team, customer needs and the value of in-person collaboration. But the harder management question comes after the schedule is set. Can employees tell what matters, who owns what, when decisions need to happen, and how they will know whether they succeeded?

Remote and hybrid work make weak management more visible because employees have fewer informal ways to repair ambiguity. Strong managers respond by making direction durable, feedback timely, and accountability explicit. That is the operating system that lets flexible work deliver loyalty and output rather than confusion and churn.

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators .”

articles.title: Thune: ‘No clear path forward’ on permanent daylight saving time legislation
articles.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) says there is “no clear path forward” to pass legislation to make daylight saving time year-round despite the strong support the legislation has from President Trump, who has stepped up pressure on GOP senators to move it. “The president feels strongly on it like he does a lot of…
articles.body:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) says there is “no clear path forward” to pass legislation to make daylight saving time year-round despite the strong support the legislation has from President Trump, who has stepped up pressure on GOP senators to move it.

“The president feels strongly on it like he does a lot of issues,” Thune told Politico. “It’s something we’re having conversations about but there’s no clear path forward or consensus on it yet.”

Trump has made the Sunshine Protection Act, which passed the House in a 308-117 vote in July, a top priority less than a month before Election Day.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“A ridiculous Clock changing process that takes place twice a year, costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine,” the president posted to Truth Social on Friday.

“People don’t want to go around changing their Clocks anymore and, besides, far and away, most people like having an hour of extra sunlight in the evening, rather than in the morning,” he added.

Trump took aim at Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) for opposing the legislation, which Cotton says has been tried before and repealed once Americans discovered the hardships of late-winter sunrises in many parts of the country.

The president claimed Cotton is blocking the bill “for reasons unknown” and posted the senator’s private cellphone number on his Truth Social account, which has more than 13 million followers, and urged people to call the Arkansas Republican and press him to drop his opposition.

“Almost everybody wants ‘The Sunshine Protection Act’ to pass, except for Tom Cotton. To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself,” he posted Saturday online.

The bill would allow states to adopt permanent daylight saving time , which is very popular in some states, such as Florida.

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) is pushing for a vote on the bill in the lame-duck session, which is scheduled for part of November and December.

“I’ve got my Sunshine Protection Act. I’m working on a vote on that. We’re going to have a vote on that. It [lets] states make their own decisions,” he told The Hill.

But the legislation faces broader opposition within the Senate GOP conference than from just Cotton.

“I think there’s more opposition to it than the president realizes,” Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) said Monday. “There’s some real safety concerns, particularly in the more northern and rural states where children get on the school bus at very early hours.”

Thune voted against making daylight saving time year-round when it came up for consideration in the Senate Commerce Committee.

“I’m from a northern clime,” he told reporters earlier this year. “I voted against it in committee.”

articles.summary: California officials denounced President Donald Trump for saying at a campaign rally in Nebraska on Monday that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego, calling his remarks “deranged” and “irresponsible.”
articles.body: California officials denounced President Donald Trump for saying at a campaign rally in Nebraska on Monday that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego, calling his remarks “deranged” and “irresponsible.” In an apparent reference to the effect of the Iran war on U.S. prices, Trump said, “Remember, with the war, it’s just artificial. It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.” “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego,” Trump said, drawing cheers from the crowd. California and the state’s leaders are a frequent target of Trump’s ire, particularly Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat who is widely viewed as potential 2028 presidential contender. In his comments at the rally, Trump appeared to be making light of the potential for Iran to attack major American cities. In response to the backlash, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said in a post on X that the controversy “is not rooted in reality.” “He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” Cheung said. “America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.” State and local officials rebuked the president over his comments. “After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom said in a post to X. “He is deranged and dangerous.” The mayors of Los Angeles and San Diego also quickly responded to the president’s remarks. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, wrote on X that Trump’s “statements against our city are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety.” “The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” Bass wrote. “In the face of irresponsible threats, as Angelenos, we know how to stand together and protect our city.” San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria, also a Democrat, said in a post to X that his city “is not collateral damage.” “We are not expendable,” Gloria added. “And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” In his remarks, Trump also said the war would be over “very soon,” something he has suggested dozens of times over the past several months. The president has argued that the war was necessary to ensure Iran could not develop a nuclear weapon. California’s Democratic senators also condemned the president’s comments. In a post on X, Sen. Alex Padilla accused Trump of “inviting an attack on U.S. soil, putting millions of Americans and hundreds of thousands of our servicemembers at risk while trying to get Americans to cheer for an attack on our own country.” “What kind of Commander in Chief does that?” Padilla added. Sen. Adam Schiff hit back at Trump’s remark that the war would end soon. “How many times have we heard that promise?” Schiff wrote on X. “And if it means attacks on two major American cities in the process, he is not troubled by the cost.” California is considered a solidly blue state and its voters supported Trump’s Democratic opponents in all three presidential elections.

articles.title: Tillis on possibility Trump doxes him: ‘I got his number too’
articles.summary: After President Trump leaked a Republican lawmaker’s phone number on social media this past weekend, Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) warned he would not withstand the same treatment. “With all due respect, I got his number too,” Tillis told the hosts of ABC’s “The View” on Monday. The Republican, who has repeatedly clashed with the president…
articles.body:
After President Trump leaked a Republican lawmaker’s phone number on social media this past weekend, Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) warned he would not withstand the same treatment.

“With all due respect, I got his number too,” Tillis told the hosts of ABC’s “The View” on Monday.

The Republican, who has repeatedly clashed with the president during the second Trump administration, was on the show to promote his new book, “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents.”

Tillis’s comment followed Trump’s repeated criticism of Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) on Saturday over the Republican senator’s opposition to a bill that would make daylight saving time the permanent standard time.

In one Truth Social post , the president posted Cotton’s phone number and told his supporters to call the lawmaker and urge him to change his stance on this legislation.

Tillis, who is retiring at the end of his current term, said on Monday he was “not at all” concerned about the potential that the president would retaliate against him for this book, which includes private text exchanges between himself and Trump.

“We could dedicate a whole show, to me, the bookends of overreach and vindictive prosecutions, et cetera,” the senator said. “For people to forget about their party’s overreach puts that party in peril in the next election. That’s my whole point.”

In the book, the GOP senator reflected on his vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, calling it the “ biggest regret ” of his career in Congress.

“The View” host Alyssa Farah Griffin pressed Tillis on the new House resolution to impeach Hegseth, which was introduced by ousted GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.).

The North Carolina senator said he did not know whether this impeachment effort would be successful but added, “I hope he gets fired.”

The Republican also praised Trump as a “great political force” during his Monday appearance on the talk show, pointing to his track record of “pulling together coalitions.”

However, Tillis noted that the president has lost some support from key voting blocs, such as among Hispanic voters.

A survey from NBC News and Telemundo found that 59 percent of Hispanic voters preferred Democrats to win the November elections over the 35 percent who favored Republicans. This voting demographic was key to Trump’s win in the 2024 presidential election.

“The support among Hispanics has almost evaporated,” Tillis said. “So the very coalitions that the president … was able to pull together are falling apart.”

articles.body:
President Trump is facing fierce backlash from California officials after suggesting Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego during a campaign rally speech Monday night in Nebraska.

Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) blasted the rhetoric as “deranged and dangerous.”

Trump’s Rapid Response account clarified his comments on X : “He was saying the U.S. is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance.”

Trump on Tuesday is set to visit Tradepoint Atlantic in Baltimore to speak at an event hosted by defense technology company Anduril Industries.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said Monday there is “no clear path forward” to pass legislation to make daylight saving time year-round despite the push from Trump .

A flurry of midterm election debates also happens this week, with Maine Senate candidates and Iowa gubernatorial hopefuls among those taking the stage Tuesday night.

A federal appeals court in Boston will hear arguments Tuesday in a lawsuit filed by groups against Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over his overhaul of the childhood vaccine schedule . The lawsuit is led by the American Academy of Pediatrics and other medical groups.

The number of recommended diseases to be vaccinated against dropped from 18 to 11 in January. A district court judge initially ruled in their favor and temporarily blocked the changes.

articles.title: Phil Collins says Trump ‘sees everything as a deal’: ‘Very scary time’
articles.summary: Phil Collins is knocking President Trump as “nasty,” saying that the commander in chief “plays politics like a businessman,” even though handling U.S. and international relations isn’t “really a business at all.” “It’s diplomacy,” Collins said in a recent interview on “Piers Morgan Uncensored.” “Sometimes you can lose, but still come out winning,” the “In…
articles.body:
Phil Collins is knocking President Trump as “nasty,” saying that the commander in chief “plays politics like a businessman,” even though handling U.S. and international relations isn’t “really a business at all.”

“It’s diplomacy,” Collins said in a recent interview on “Piers Morgan Uncensored.”

“Sometimes you can lose, but still come out winning,” the “In the Air Tonight” singer said.

But the president, Collins said, “Sees everything as a deal — won or lost — and I think it’s a very scary time.”

“His whole manner is unattractive,” the former Genesis frontman said.

“Historically, presidents have been eloquent and elegant. You feel like even if you don’t agree with them, you still respect them,” the 75-year-old English performer said.

“But when someone like Trump is as nasty as he is, you end up feeling dislike for him,” Collins told host Piers Morgan.

“It’s very scary with what’s happening,” Collins said.

“It wouldn’t surprise me if if he just tries to overrule the two-term deal — American presidents can only serve two terms,” Collins said in a reference to the Constitution’s 22 nd Amendment barring a president from serving more than two terms.

Trump has repeatedly teased the idea of launching a third term bid, but has also acknowledged that the Constitution is “pretty clear” that he is not allowed to run again.

“I don’t think he will do that. I don’t think the system would let him,” Morgan replied.

Saying he’s known Trump a “long time,” Morgan added, “The one thing I’ve learned is never to be surprised by him because nothing is surprising. In other words, he can basically do anything.”

“I don’t think he would be allowed to do that. I think even his own party, even his own followers, would disagree with that suggestion,” the Grammy Award winner said of Trump seeking a third term.

articles.title: Top Republican super PAC pledges $5 million for South Carolina Senate race
articles.summary: The top Republican super PAC involved in Senate races is planning to spend $5 million in South Carolina, a source familiar with the spending confirmed.
articles.body: The top Republican super PAC involved in Senate races is planning to spend $5 million in South Carolina, a source familiar with the spending confirmed to NBC News on Tuesday. The injection of funds from the Senate Leadership Fund, a group aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is the latest sign that the race between GOP Sen. Darline Graham and Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews is competitive. The outlay was first reported by Axios. It comes as the Senate map is shifting further in Democrats’ favor, putting Republican-leaning states increasingly in play with less than a month remaining until Election Day. Trump carried South Carolina by 18 points in 2024. The last Democrat elected to represent South Carolina in the Senate was Fritz Hollings, who served from 1966 until 2005. Asked about SLF’s decision, Graham campaign spokesperson T.W. Arrighi said in a statement, “After over a month of non-stop misleading ads from Annie Andrews, funded by millions of out-of-state dollars, South Carolinians are beginning to learn the truth.” The Andrews campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham to the seat soon after her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, died suddenly in July. Within days, Darline Graham announced she would run for a full six-year Senate term with the backing of President Donald Trump. Graham became the GOP Senate nominee after she defeated Rep. Ralph Norman in a primary runoff in August. The president has campaigned for Graham and used an anti-trans slur to attack Andrews on Monday in a Truth Social post by referring to her three times as “trannie.” Andrews is not transgender. An outside GOP group, Security is Strength, also launched an attack ad against Andrews on Monday focused on transgender issues. But it’s Andrews who has been dominating the airwaves so far this fall. Since the beginning of September, Andrews’ campaign has spent $6.1 million on ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. That’s nearly 10 times more than the $687,000 in ads from outside Republican groups. Graham’s own campaign has not spend any significant funds on ads since the August primary runoff. The new spending underscores how races that were previously considered competitive — like the Senate matchup in North Carolina between Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley, and the Georgia race between Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Rep. Mike Collins — are now viewed as leaning toward Democrats. The Senate race in solid red Kansas between GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton also has tightened. In response to that changing dynamic, the Senate Leadership Fund canceled its ad spending in North Carolina’s Senate race last week and launched a new ad campaign in Kansas.

articles.title: Tillis: ‘Almost statistically impossible’ for Republicans to win House in midterms
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Monday it is “almost statistically impossible” for the Republican Party to retain control of the House in the 2026 midterm elections. Appearing on MS NOW’s “The Beat,” host Ari Melber asked the senator about divisions within the GOP driven by President Trump. “I’m supporting the president because he’s the head…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Monday it is “almost statistically impossible” for the Republican Party to retain control of the House in the 2026 midterm elections.

Appearing on MS NOW’s “The Beat,” host Ari Melber asked the senator about divisions within the GOP driven by President Trump.

“I’m supporting the president because he’s the head of the party, not because he’s Donald J. Trump, but because he is the face of our party,” Tillis said. “And I want my party to be in the best position for elections. And we’re going to, we’re going to take a little bit of a hit this season and recover from it, I believe.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Tillis, who is not running for reelection, added: “I think the House is almost statistically impossible to win at this point.”

He continued that he believed Republicans would retain control of the Senate but “it will be a tight margin, but I still think we pull it out.”

“Because we’ve got great candidates in Maine, Ohio, Arkansas. They’ve just got to run hard and we’ve got to support them,” he said.

Tillis’s remarks come as GOP candidates are grappling with a midterm environment where Trump’s low approval ratings , an unpopular war in Iran, a tariff war with Canada and inflation where cost of living remains a concern.

The Senate is considered a toss-up by polling averages.

The Democratic Party needs to win at least four seats to regain control of the upper chamber ; races in Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, Texas and Alaska remain competitive, according to recent polling from The New York Times/Siena .

It found Democrats leading by 6 points in the Texas Senate race, 7 points in Alaska and 3 points in Ohio. The party’s candidates are down 1 point in Iowa and tied in Kansas. With the surveys in Ohio, Iowa and Kansas falling within the margin of error — 4.5 points in Ohio, and 4.6 points in both Iowa and Kansas — those races are essentially tied.

Tillis’s open seat will likely go to Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), which gives him an 84 percent probability of flipping the seat.

DDHQ also forecasts that Democrats have a 76 percent probability of flipping the House and a 56 percent chance of taking back the Senate.

articles.title: DOJ files record number of cases to strip Americans of citizenship
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed a record number of cases to strip Americans of citizenship, the department said Monday. In a Monday press release, the department said it unveiled on Monday the filing of denaturalization actions targeting 40 people “accused of serious offenses.” The filings occurred in a number of U.S. district courts,…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed a record number of cases to strip Americans of citizenship, the department said Monday.

In a Monday press release , the department said it unveiled on Monday the filing of denaturalization actions targeting 40 people “accused of serious offenses.”

The filings occurred in a number of U.S. district courts, with the offenses involving acting as an agent for a foreign government and committing voluntary manslaughter, per the DOJ.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The department also said in the release that the actions were filed from late August to early October, and “represent the largest volume of complaints submitted in a single period under the Trump administration.”

“Today’s announcement marks the largest denaturalization effort in modern history,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the release.

“From an individual convicted of espionage to others convicted of sexual offenses against minors, these defendants concealed critical facts from the U.S. government and represent serious criminal offenders,” he added.

The denaturalization of citizens not born in the U.S. is uncommon, and really only occurs in cases in which a person committed fraud to try and immigrate to the U.S., or if they committed a type of disqualifying crime.

According to prior research , between 1990 and 2018, there were only 305 denaturalization cases brought by the government.

The second Trump administration has cracked down on immigration but has received strong backlash for its tactics.

Multiple people have been fatally shot in encounters with federal immigration authorities within the last year, and there have been complaints about how those authorities treat those they detain.

articles.title: 86 percent think taxpayer-funded, campaign-style Trump ads inappropriate: Survey
articles.summary: An overwhelming majority of Americans in a new poll released Monday said the Trump administration’s use of taxpayer dollars to fund campaign-style TV advertisements was inappropriate. The Reuters/Ipsos survey found that 86 percent of U.S. adults disapproved of the use of taxpayer money for the $20 million ad campaign, with only 9 percent in support…
articles.body:
An overwhelming majority of Americans in a new poll released Monday said the Trump administration’s use of taxpayer dollars to fund campaign-style TV advertisements was inappropriate.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey found that 86 percent of U.S. adults disapproved of the use of taxpayer money for the $20 million ad campaign , with only 9 percent in support of the move.

President Trump recently walked back the decision after a wave of backlash that included Republican allies . The 30-second commercial features a voiceover of Trump pushing back on the influence of communism, socialism and Marxism in the U.S. ahead of the midterm elections.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters last week the ads carried a “great message” but criticized the use of taxpayer funds.

GOP Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.) agreed, recently telling the media it was “not something I would have done.”

“I just don’t think it’s right to be using taxpayer money in that way,” he said. “I think they need to rethink that strategy.”

Richard Painter, former White House ethics attorney, suggested that the use of taxpayer dollars for these ad spots could be “an impeachable offense.”

The president said Monday that his super PAC, MAGA, Inc., will fund the future “Patriotic Ads” following this backlash.

“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

“This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” he added.

The survey also polled respondents about their opinions on federal institutions being named after a sitting U.S. president, with 72 expressing broad disapproval of the action. The Trump administration has pushed to add the president’s name to institutions like the Kennedy Center and the U.S. Institute of Peace .

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted among 4,506 U.S. adults from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5. It has a margin of error of approximately 2 percentage points.

articles.title: White House pushes back on characterization of Trump’s Iran comments on LA, San Diego
articles.summary: The White House pushed back on critics’ characterization of President Trump’s comments at a rally on Monday evening suggesting Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego. “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote in a post on X on Tuesday. “He…
articles.body:
The White House pushed back on critics’ characterization of President Trump’s comments at a rally on Monday evening suggesting Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.

“The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote in a post on X on Tuesday.

“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money,” he continued.

The White House’s Rapid Response X account hit back at a Los Angeles Times post on X, which said Trump suggested “letting Iran take out” the California cities.

“No, he didn’t, you buffoons. He was saying the U.S. is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance,” the White House post read.

Trump originally made the remarks at a midterm rally in Grand Island, Nebraska.

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe,” the president said, apparently speaking about the Iran war, before adding that Iran could “take out a city.”

“Let ‘em take out Los Angeles, let ‘em take out San Diego,” he continued. “This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”

The comments elicited backlash from Golden State Democrats, including Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), who is exploring a 2028 presidential run.

“After sending the National Guard to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” the governor wrote in a social media post. “He is deranged and dangerous.”

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) called the comments “dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety,” while San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria (D) said in his own statement the city was “not collateral damage.”

articles.title: Sabato’s Crystal Ball moves Alaska Senate race to ‘leans Democrat’
articles.summary: Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an election handicapper based at the University of Virginia, has shifted its race rating for the Alaska Senate race to be more optimistic for Democrats. The outlet moved the race to “Leans Democrat” from “Toss-up,” showing that polling data and other indicators are increasingly suggesting former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) could topple…
articles.body:
Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an election handicapper based at the University of Virginia, has shifted its race rating for the Alaska Senate race to be more optimistic for Democrats.

The outlet moved the race to “Leans Democrat” from “Toss-up,” showing that polling data and other indicators are increasingly suggesting former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) could topple incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska).

“Sullivan, as an incumbent without any obvious scandals, still has some advantages, aside from the state’s red terrain,” wrote J. Miles Coleman and Kyle Kondik in a press release announcing the shift. They mentioned the state’s over-45 population, which is still predominately swinging for Sullivan.

“But our general sense for months has been that Alaska, a small, quirky state with a unique election system, was perhaps the most promising red state Senate target for Democrats.”

Despite the rating change, the race is still very competitive. Alaska is generally a red state, national Republicans are still spending plenty of money to attack Peltola’s record, and Trump surrogates, most notably Vice President JD Vance, are stumping for Sullivan there .

Decision Desk HQ, another election handicapper, also has Peltola slightly favored to win. The other big name in election ratings, Cook Political Report , still has the race as a toss-up.

Peltola is a unique candidate as a centrist Democrat, Alaska Native and former congresswoman who was already elected statewide twice. She’s running on a campaign slogan of “fish, family and freedom,” vowing to fight corporate interests and solve Alaska’s resource problems. Sullivan has emphasized his service in the Senate passing legislation that benefited industries and veterans, among other groups, in Alaska.

Democrats need to net four Senate seats to take the majority in the midterm elections. North Carolina appears to be their best chance of winning a seat, but races in seats held by Republicans in Maine, Ohio, Texas and Iowa are also seen as toss-ups by Cook.

Democrats are defending seats in two other races listed by Cook as toss-ups in Michigan and New Hampshire.

Republicans are favored to hold a Senate seat in Kansas, though the race in that state is increasingly seen as competitive. Democrats are favored in races in Minnesota and Georgia, though both are seen as competitive.

articles.title: Racist policy caused climate vulnerability. Restorative policy is the remedy.
articles.summary: Climate adaptation must become a civil rights project.
articles.body:
Last month, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals delivered a sobering message to residents of Jackson, Mississippi, who had sued over the city’s troubled water system. The residents alleged government failures had exposed them to lead-contaminated drinking water that officials assured them was safe. Unfortunately, they did not get the remedy they sought.

This decision raises a critical question: What does justice require when the government has helped create conditions that make a community vulnerable in the first place?

Climate change does not arrive on neutral ground. Its threats are colliding with a geography of vulnerability and inequality that America spent generations constructing. During the era of legal segregation, policies including redlining racially restrictive covenants, exclusionary zoning, discriminatory lending and infrastructure development helped confine Black families to neighborhoods more likely to be flood-prone, polluted, near industrial facilities or otherwise environmentally vulnerable. The end of formal segregation did not erase that geography.

In many Black communities, segregation was followed by decades of public and private disinvestment . Water systems aged. Drainage infrastructure deteriorated. Housing declined. Trees and green spaces disappeared or were never planted. Public transportation suffered. Municipal tax bases eroded.

And neglect was only half of the story. Even as governments failed to invest adequately in Black communities, they continued to ask those communities to bear a disproportionate share of society’s burdens. Highways tore through Black neighborhoods. Polluting industries clustered nearby. We constructed inequality and vulnerability layer by layer.

Now climate change is colliding with everything we built. A neighborhood with inadequate drainage becomes more vulnerable as extreme rainfall intensifies. A community with few trees and acres of heat-absorbing pavement becomes more dangerous as temperatures rise. An aging electrical grid becomes more consequential when extreme heat makes air conditioning a matter of life and death. Fragile water systems become more precarious under flooding, drought and other climate stresses.

And families denied generations of wealth accumulation have fewer resources to evacuate, rebuild, absorb rising utility and insurance costs or move somewhere safer. Climate change did not create these inequalities. But it is magnifying them.

There is another collision we have tried to ignore — between climate change and our nation’s extraordinary capacity to tolerate Black suffering. In addition to the residents of Jackson, think of Flint, Michigan , where residents spent years fighting for safe drinking water, or Gary, Indiana , where for nearly two weeks in August residents had no power — all while a private utility worked its way, unhurried, through a restoration list.

Different cities. Different systems. But they raise the same disturbing question: What conditions have we decided are acceptable when the people living with them are Black? There are communities whose suffering triggers urgent intervention and others whose suffering becomes part of the background. Climate change threatens to make the consequences of that hierarchy far more severe.

And even our responses to climate change risk reproducing those hierarchies. Governments will spend enormous sums strengthening electrical grids, modernizing water systems, improving drainage, protecting coastlines, planting trees and rebuilding transportation infrastructure. If we follow the patterns of the past, communities with the most wealth and political power will receive protection first and recover fastest.

Climate adaptation must become a civil rights project. That means identifying vulnerability before disaster strikes and directing investment toward communities where segregation, disinvestment, environmental burdens and infrastructure neglect have compounded over generations. It means rebuilding water and energy systems, strengthening housing, improving drainage, expanding green infrastructure and ensuring reliable transportation. And it means giving residents meaningful power over the investments that will determine whether their communities survive and whether they can remain to enjoy the benefits.

The vulnerability facing many Black communities was not inevitable. It was built through decisions about where people could live, where the government would invest, where infrastructure would be placed, which communities would be protected and which could be neglected.

Generations of policy helped construct vulnerability. Governments now have an obligation to construct resilience. The climate crisis is going to force America to build. We will spend billions deciding which places to protect, which infrastructure to strengthen, and which communities to prepare for a more dangerous future.

The question is not whether we will build. It is whether we will reproduce the racial geography we inherited — or finally begin to dismantle it.

We built this vulnerability. Now we have to build something different.

Deborah Archer is president of the American Civil Liberties Union and a professor of law at New York University.

articles.title: Cotton’s opponent: ‘Not once’ has daylight savings come up on campaign trail
articles.summary: Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) Democratic opponent Hallie Shoffner said on Tuesday that “not once” has daylight savings come up on the campaign trail, after President Trump aired his frustration over stalled legislation that would make daylight saving time permanent. In an interview on MS NOW, Shoffner stated that, “I’ll tell you, over the 450 days…
articles.body:
Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) Democratic opponent Hallie Shoffner said on Tuesday that “not once” has daylight savings come up on the campaign trail, after President Trump aired his frustration over stalled legislation that would make daylight saving time permanent.

In an interview on MS NOW , Shoffner stated that, “I’ll tell you, over the 450 days that I’ve been on the campaign trail, not once have I been asked about daylight savings time.”

“I mean, what Arkansans are talking about? They’re talking about gas prices and grocery prices. They’re talking about healthcare,” she added.

Cotton is opposed to making daylight savings time permanent, arguing it would force many in Arkansas to endure dark days in getting to school.

Trump on Saturday posted Cotton’s cellphone number on his Truth Social account while attacking the Arkansas senator over his position on the bill. Trump asked his Arkansas supporters to press Cotton, the third-ranking member of the Senate GOP leadership and the chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, to drop his opposition to the Sunshine Protection Act.

Trump further blamed Cotton for the bill — which he called the “No More Changing of Clocks Act” — stalling in the Senate after it passed the House in a 308-117 vote in July.

Cotton defended his opposition to the legislation on social media , saying, “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter.”

“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” the senator concluded.

Other GOP senators backed Cotton’s position including Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) who believed “there’s more opposition to it than the president realizes,” referring to the bill.

The Arkansas Senate Race is designated as “solid Republican” by Cook Political Report . Decision Desk HQ also gives Cotton a 96 percent probability of keeping his seat for a third term over Shoffner.
